u:apt-1-percentage-change-increase-decre.title: Percentage change (increase/decrease)
u:apt-1-percentage-change-increase-decre.summary: Percentage change is always measured against the original value.

blocks.text: **% change = (change / original value) x 100.** The denominator is always the ORIGINAL (starting) value, not the new one — the most common error.
Increase from 40 to 50: change = 10, original = 40, so 10/40 x 100 = 25% increase. Decrease from 50 to 40: 10/50 x 100 = 20% decrease. Note the two are NOT equal — the base differs.
A rise of x% followed by a fall of x% never returns to the original (the base changed). This asymmetry powers many trick questions.

u:apt-2-successive-percentage-change.title: Successive percentage change
u:apt-2-successive-percentage-change.summary: Chain changes multiply; combine two with a + b + ab/100.

blocks.text: For two successive changes of a% and b%, the net change = **a + b + (ab/100)** percent. Use + for increase, - for decrease.
A 20% increase then a 10% increase: net = 20 + 10 + (20x10)/100 = 32%. A 20% increase then a 20% decrease: 20 - 20 + (20 x -20)/100 = -4% (a net 4% decrease).
Equivalently, multiply factors: (1 + a/100)(1 + b/100). This scales to any number of successive changes — just multiply all the factors.

u:apt-3-reversal-increase-then-decrease-.title: Reversal - increase then decrease to original
u:apt-3-reversal-increase-then-decrease-.summary: To undo an x% increase you need a smaller percentage decrease, and vice versa.

blocks.text: If a value is increased by x%, the % decrease needed to return to the original is **[x/(100+x)] x 100**. If decreased by x%, the increase needed back is **[x/(100-x)] x 100**.
Price up 25%: to restore, decrease by 25/125 x 100 = 20%. Price down 20%: to restore, increase by 20/80 x 100 = 25%. The percentages differ because the base changed.
The reversal percentage is always relative to the NEW (changed) base, which is why it's smaller after an increase and larger after a decrease.

A salary was cut by 20%. What increase restores it?

u:apt-4-net-effect-formula.title: Net effect formula
u:apt-4-net-effect-formula.summary: Combine two independent percentage effects with x + y + xy/100.

blocks.text: When two quantities each change (e.g. price and quantity affecting expenditure, or length and breadth affecting area), the net percentage effect = **x + y + (xy/100)**, with signs for increase/decrease.
If a rectangle's length rises 20% and breadth falls 10%, area change = 20 - 10 + (20 x -10)/100 = 10 - 2 = +8%. Expenditure = price% + quantity% + product.
This is the same formula as successive change — because two multiplicative effects on a product combine identically. Recognising the 'two factors multiplied' pattern is the skill.

u:apt-5-population-growth-and-depreciati.title: Population growth and depreciation
u:apt-5-population-growth-and-depreciati.summary: Compound growth/decay: multiply by (1 +/- r/100) each period.

blocks.text: **Growth**: Final = Initial x (1 + r/100)^n. **Depreciation** (decay): Final = Initial x (1 - r/100)^n. Here r = rate per period, n = number of periods — identical to compound interest.
Population 10000 growing 10%/year for 2 years: 10000 x (1.1)^2 = 12100. A machine worth 50000 depreciating 20%/year for 2 years: 50000 x (0.8)^2 = 32000.
This is compound interest in disguise. If growth and decline alternate (up r% then down r%), the net is a decrease (same as the increase-then-decrease reversal).

Population/depreciation problems use the same formula as:
mcqs.explain: Both compound each period by (1 +/- r/100)^n.

u:apt-6-marks-passing-percentage-exam-pr.title: Marks, passing percentage, exam problems
u:apt-6-marks-passing-percentage-exam-pr.summary: Use the pass-mark relationship to find maximum marks from a fail margin.

blocks.text: Typical setup: a student scores S marks and fails by F marks, where pass mark = p% of maximum M. Then **p% of M = S + F**, so M = (S + F) x 100 / p.
Scored 120, fails by 30, pass is 40%: pass mark = 150, so 40% of M = 150, M = 375. If two students' data is given (one passes by a, one fails by b), set the pass marks equal to solve.
The key relation: pass mark = score + fail-margin = score - pass-margin. Convert the percentage pass requirement into an equation for M.

u:apt-7-price-consumption-inverse-relati.title: Price-consumption inverse relation
u:apt-7-price-consumption-inverse-relati.summary: To keep spending fixed when price rises x%, cut consumption by x/(100+x).

blocks.text: Expenditure = Price x Consumption. To keep expenditure constant when price rises by x%, reduce consumption by **[x/(100+x)] x 100 %**. When price falls x%, you can increase consumption by [x/(100-x)] x 100%.
Petrol price up 25%: to keep the bill unchanged, cut usage by 25/125 x 100 = 20%. This is exactly the reversal formula, because price and consumption are inversely proportional at fixed expenditure.
Recognise it as the increase-then-decrease reversal: raising one factor by x% requires lowering the other by x/(100+x) to keep the product constant.

u:apt-8-error-percentage.title: Error percentage
u:apt-8-error-percentage.summary: Error % = (error / actual) x 100 - useful in measurement and DI problems.

blocks.text: **Error % = (|measured - actual| / actual) x 100.** The denominator is the ACTUAL (true) value. Common in measurement mistakes and approximation questions.

If someone multiplies by 5/6 instead of 6/5, compare the two results: error = |correct - wrong|/correct. When a value should be multiplied by a but is divided instead, work out both and take the difference over the correct one.

Always divide the error by the CORRECT value, not the wrong one. Errors in area from a length error compound via the net-effect formula (a length error of x% gives roughly 2x% area error for small x).

u:apt-9-percentage-in-data-interpretatio.title: Percentage in Data Interpretation
u:apt-9-percentage-in-data-interpretatio.summary: Most DI questions reduce to percentage comparisons and share-of-total calculations.

blocks.text: In **Data Interpretation**, percentages appear constantly: share of total, percentage change between years, and percentage comparison between categories. Speed comes from percentage fluency, not new theory.

items: **Share of total** = (part / total) x 100.
**% change year over year** = (new - old)/old x 100.
**Comparison** = 'A is what % of B' = A/B x 100; 'A is what % more than B' = (A-B)/B x 100.

blocks.text: Approximate aggressively in DI: round values, use fraction equivalents (e.g. treat 33% as 1/3), and compare rather than compute exactly when options are far apart. Time saved matters more than precision.

u:apt-10-bodmas.title: BODMAS
u:apt-10-bodmas.summary: The order of operations: Brackets, Orders, Division/Multiplication, Addition/Subtraction.

blocks.text: **BODMAS** dictates the order to evaluate expressions: **B**rackets, **O**rders (powers/roots), **D**ivision and **M**ultiplication (left to right), **A**ddition and **S**ubtraction (left to right).
Division and multiplication have EQUAL precedence — evaluate left to right, not division first. Same for addition and subtraction. e.g. 8 / 4 x 2 = (8/4) x 2 = 4, not 8/(4x2)=1.
The common mistake is treating M before D or A before S. They pair at equal precedence and are done left to right. Innermost brackets first.

mcqs.q: Evaluate 12 / 4 x 3:
mcqs.explain: Left to right: (12/4) x 3 = 3 x 3 = 9. D and M are equal precedence.

mcqs.q: Evaluate 2 + 3 x 4:
mcqs.explain: Multiplication before addition: 3x4=12, then 2+12=14.

mcqs.q: In BODMAS, division and multiplication are:
options: Equal precedence, done left to right
mcqs.explain: They share precedence and are evaluated left to right.

u:apt-11-surds-and-indices.title: Surds and indices
u:apt-11-surds-and-indices.summary: The laws of exponents and roots that simplify powers quickly.

blocks.text: **Index laws**: a^m x a^n = a^(m+n); a^m / a^n = a^(m-n); (a^m)^n = a^(mn); a^0 = 1; a^(-n) = 1/a^n. **Surds**: a^(1/n) is the nth root; sqrt(a) x sqrt(b) = sqrt(ab).
Rationalise a surd denominator by multiplying by the conjugate: 1/(sqrt3 - 1) x (sqrt3 + 1)/(sqrt3 + 1) = (sqrt3 + 1)/2. Convert roots to fractional powers to apply index laws.
Same base → add/subtract exponents; power of a power → multiply. Fractional exponents are roots. These few laws solve most surd/index questions.

mcqs.q: Simplify 2^3 x 2^4:
mcqs.explain: Same base: add exponents, 2^(3+4) = 2^7.

mcqs.q: (3^2)^3 equals:
mcqs.explain: Power of a power multiplies exponents: 3^(2x3) = 3^6.

mcqs.q: a^(-2) is equal to:
mcqs.explain: A negative exponent is the reciprocal: a^(-n) = 1/a^n.

u:apt-12-approximation-techniques.title: Approximation techniques
u:apt-12-approximation-techniques.summary: Round smartly and estimate to pick answers fast without full computation.

blocks.text: In 'approximate value' questions, exact arithmetic wastes time. **Round** numbers to convenient values, compute, and match the closest option.

u:apt-13-fractions-to-decimals-shortcuts.summary: Memorised fraction-decimal equivalents make comparison and computation instant.

blocks.text: Knowing common **fraction = decimal = percent** conversions by heart speeds up comparisons and calculations enormously.
To compare fractions quickly, cross-multiply (a/b vs c/d: compare ad vs bc) or convert to known decimals. To compare 5/7 and 7/9: 5x9=45 vs 7x7=49, so 7/9 is larger.

u:apt-15-simple-ratio.title: Simple ratio
u:apt-15-simple-ratio.summary: A ratio compares quantities; scale both parts by the same factor to keep it equal.

blocks.text: A **ratio** a:b compares two quantities of the same kind. It equals the fraction a/b and is unchanged when both terms are multiplied/divided by the same number (so simplify to lowest terms).
If a:b = 3:4 and the total is 35, each 'part' = 35/(3+4) = 5, so a = 15, b = 20. Add the ratio terms to find the value of one part.
Convert a ratio problem to 'parts': total parts = sum of ratio terms; value per part = total/parts. Then each quantity = its ratio number x value-per-part.

u:apt-16-compound-ratio.title: Compound ratio
u:apt-16-compound-ratio.summary: Multiply ratios term by term to compound them.

blocks.text: The **compound ratio** of a:b and c:d is **(a x c):(b x d)** — multiply the antecedents together and the consequents together. Related: duplicate ratio = a^2:b^2; sub-duplicate = sqrt(a):sqrt(b).
Compound of 2:3 and 4:5 = (2x4):(3x5) = 8:15. Compounding chains: for three ratios, multiply all antecedents and all consequents.
Compounding = term-wise multiplication. Duplicate/triplicate ratios are squares/cubes of the terms; sub-duplicate/sub-triplicate are the roots.

The duplicate ratio of 3:5 is:
mcqs.explain: Duplicate ratio squares the terms: 3^2:5^2 = 9:25.

options: Multiply antecedents together and consequents together
mcqs.explain: Compound ratio is (a x c):(b x d).

u:apt-17-direct-and-inverse-proportion.title: Direct and inverse proportion
u:apt-17-direct-and-inverse-proportion.summary: Direct: both rise together (ratio constant). Inverse: one rises as the other falls (product constant).

blocks.text: **Direct proportion**: y = kx (y/x constant) — more workers, more output. **Inverse proportion**: xy = k (product constant) — more workers, less time.
Direct: if 5 pens cost 40, 8 pens cost 40/5 x 8 = 64. Inverse: if 6 workers finish in 10 days, 4 workers take 6 x 10 / 4 = 15 days (fewer workers → more time).
Identify the relationship first: do the quantities move together (direct) or oppositely (inverse)? Direct keeps the RATIO constant; inverse keeps the PRODUCT constant.

mcqs.q: If 8 machines produce 240 units, how many do 5 machines produce (same rate)?
mcqs.explain: Direct proportion: 240/8 x 5 = 150.

mcqs.q: 6 pipes fill a tank in 8 hours. How long for 4 pipes?
mcqs.explain: Inverse proportion: 6 x 8 / 4 = 12 hours.

mcqs.q: In inverse proportion, the quantity that stays constant is the:
mcqs.explain: Inverse proportion means x times y is constant.

u:apt-18-dividing-a-quantity-in-a-ratio.title: Dividing a quantity in a ratio
u:apt-18-dividing-a-quantity-in-a-ratio.summary: Split a total by giving each share its ratio-fraction of the whole.

blocks.text: To divide amount T in ratio a:b:c, each share = its term / (a+b+c) x T. The value of **one part** = T / (a+b+c).
Divide 900 among A:B:C = 2:3:4. Total parts = 9, each part = 100, so A=200, B=300, C=400. For 'A gets 50 more than B' style, translate the extra into parts and solve.
Always sum the ratio terms first to find one part's value. Then multiply each term by it. This handles any number of shares.

mcqs.q: Divide 1200 among A:B:C = 1:2:3. C's share is:
To divide a quantity in a ratio, first find:
options: The value of one part (total / sum of terms)
mcqs.explain: One part = total divided by the sum of ratio terms; each share is its term times that.

mcqs.q: Divide 480 in ratio 3:5. The smaller share is:
mcqs.explain: Parts = 8, each = 60; smaller = 3 x 60 = 180.

u:apt-19-ratio-with-age-mixture-overlap.title: Ratio with age/mixture overlap
u:apt-19-ratio-with-age-mixture-overlap.summary: Many age and mixture problems are ratio problems in disguise - set up 'x parts'.

blocks.text: Ratios appear across topics. **Ages**: 'ages are in ratio 3:4, sum 35' → parts of 5, ages 15 and 20. **Mixtures**: milk:water ratios combine via ratio arithmetic. The trick is expressing quantities as multiples of a common variable x.
If present ages are 3x and 5x and in 5 years the ratio becomes 2:3, write (3x+5)/(5x+5) = 2/3 and solve. Turning ratios into '3x, 5x' variables converts word problems into simple equations.
The universal move: let the ratio terms be 3x, 4x, ... then use the extra condition (a sum, a change over time, a mixture) to solve for x. Ratios are the scaffolding for age and mixture problems.

mcqs.explain: Parts = 9, each = 7; younger = 4 x 7 = 28.

options: Let the terms be multiples of x (3x, 4x...) and solve
mcqs.explain: Expressing ratio terms as 3x, 4x turns conditions into a solvable equation.

u:apt-20-componendo-and-dividendo.title: Componendo and dividendo
u:apt-20-componendo-and-dividendo.summary: A ratio shortcut: if a/b = c/d then (a+b)/(a-b) = (c+d)/(c-d).

blocks.text: **Componendo-dividendo**: if a/b = c/d, then **(a+b)/(a-b) = (c+d)/(c-d)**. It's a fast way to solve proportion equations that would otherwise need cross-multiplication and algebra.

If (x+2)/(x-2) = 7/3, treat as a/b form: by componendo-dividendo the sum/difference relationship lets you jump to x quickly. Useful when both numerator and denominator contain the unknown symmetrically.
Componendo alone: a/b = c/d → (a+b)/b = (c+d)/d. Dividendo: (a-b)/b = (c-d)/d. Combined gives the (a+b)/(a-b) form. It saves steps on ratio/proportion equations.

u:apt-21-cp-sp-profit-loss-percent.title: CP, SP, profit/loss percent
u:apt-21-cp-sp-profit-loss-percent.summary: Profit and loss are always calculated on the cost price.

blocks.text: **Profit = SP - CP; Loss = CP - SP.** Crucially, **profit% and loss% are on the COST PRICE**: Profit% = (Profit/CP) x 100. So SP = CP x (1 + profit%/100).
CP 200, SP 250: profit = 50, profit% = 50/200 x 100 = 25%. To find CP from SP and profit%: CP = SP x 100/(100 + profit%). CP 200 sold at 25% profit → SP = 200 x 1.25 = 250.
The default base is cost price (unless stated otherwise). Mixing up CP and SP as the base is the top profit/loss error.

u:apt-22-successive-discounts.title: Successive discounts
u:apt-22-successive-discounts.summary: Two discounts combine like successive percentage changes: a + b - ab/100.

blocks.text: Two successive discounts of a% and b% give a single equivalent discount of **a + b - (ab/100)** percent (both are decreases). Apply to the marked price.
Discounts of 20% and 10%: equivalent = 20 + 10 - (20x10)/100 = 28% (not 30%). Final price = MP x 0.8 x 0.9 = MP x 0.72.
Successive discounts are NOT additive — they're less than the sum because the second applies to an already-reduced price. Multiply the (1 - d/100) factors for the exact result.

u:apt-23-marked-price-and-discount-chain.title: Marked price and discount chains
u:apt-23-marked-price-and-discount-chain.summary: Relate marked price, discount, and selling price - and profit still hinges on cost price.

blocks.text: **SP = MP x (1 - discount%/100).** The marked price (list price) is what's before discount. Profit is still on CP: a seller marks up over CP, then gives a discount, and the net can still be a profit.
CP 100, marked 40% above (MP=140), discount 25%: SP = 140 x 0.75 = 105, so profit = 5%. Chain: CP → markup → MP → discount → SP → compare to CP for profit.
Track two separate percentages: markup (MP over CP) and discount (SP off MP). The actual profit depends on both plus the cost price base.

u:apt-24-dishonest-dealer-false-weights.summary: Using a lighter weight creates extra profit: gain% = error/(true - error) x 100.

blocks.text: A dealer who sells using a **false (lighter) weight** while charging for the full amount makes hidden profit. If he uses w grams instead of 1000 g (claiming a kg), **gain% = (1000 - w)/w x 100** (selling at cost price otherwise).
Uses 900 g for a 'kilo': gain% = (1000-900)/900 x 100 = 11.11%. Gain% = error / true value given, where the base is what the customer actually receives.
The base for the gain is the ACTUAL quantity given (w), not the claimed 1000. If the dealer ALSO marks up, combine the two profit effects via the net-effect formula.

u:apt-26-break-even-and-multiple-article.title: Break-even and multiple articles
u:apt-26-break-even-and-multiple-article.summary: Break-even is zero profit; 'CP of x = SP of y' problems compare per-unit prices.

blocks.text: **Break-even** is where SP = CP (no profit, no loss). A common type: 'the CP of X articles equals the SP of Y articles' → profit% = (X - Y)/Y x 100.
If CP of 20 articles = SP of 16 articles: profit% = (20-16)/16 x 100 = 25%. (More cost-articles than sell-articles for the same money means profit.)
For 'CP of X = SP of Y', the sign of (X - Y) tells profit (positive) or loss (negative), and the base is Y. Break-even occurs when X = Y.

u:apt-27-simple-partnership.title: Simple partnership
u:apt-27-simple-partnership.summary: When capital is invested for the same time, profit splits in the ratio of investments.

blocks.text: In a **simple partnership**, partners invest for the **same duration**, so profit is shared in the ratio of their **capitals**. Profit share of A = (A's capital / total capital) x total profit.
A invests 5000, B invests 3000 for the same time, profit 4000: ratio 5:3, so A gets 5/8 x 4000 = 2500, B gets 1500.
Equal time → share in the ratio of investments alone. This is the base case; time-weighting (below) generalises it.

u:apt-28-compound-partnership-time-weigh.title: Compound partnership (time-weighted)
u:apt-28-compound-partnership-time-weigh.summary: When durations differ, profit splits in the ratio of capital x time.

blocks.text: In a **compound partnership**, partners invest for **different times**, so profit is shared in the ratio of **capital x time** (money-months). Share ratio = (C1 x T1) : (C2 x T2) : ...
A invests 8000 for 6 months, B invests 6000 for 8 months: ratio = (8000x6):(6000x8) = 48000:48000 = 1:1, so profit splits equally despite unequal capital.
The unit is capital-time (money x months). Always multiply each partner's investment by how long it was invested before forming the ratio.

u:apt-29-working-vs-sleeping-partner.title: Working vs sleeping partner
u:apt-29-working-vs-sleeping-partner.summary: A working partner may take a salary/commission first; the rest splits by investment-time.

blocks.text: A **working partner** actively manages the business and often receives a **salary or a commission** (a % of profit) before the remaining profit is divided. A **sleeping partner** only invests capital.

Order: deduct the working partner's salary/commission from total profit first, then split the REMAINING profit in the capital-time ratio. The working partner's total = their salary/commission + their capital share.
Handle special payments (salary, commission) BEFORE the ratio split. Only the balance is divided in proportion to investment-time.

mcqs.q: A working partner's salary/commission is:
options: Deducted from profit before the remainder is split by investment
Equal to the sleeping partner's share

options: Only invests capital and shares profit accordingly
mcqs.explain: A sleeping partner contributes only capital and shares profit by investment.

mcqs.explain: Commission 1000; remaining 9000 splits 4500 each; working partner = 1000 + 4500 = 5500.

u:apt-30-profit-sharing-with-varying-inv.title: Profit sharing with varying investment
u:apt-30-profit-sharing-with-varying-inv.summary: If a partner changes their capital mid-year, sum capital x time over each period.

blocks.text: When a partner **adds or withdraws capital** partway through, compute their total **capital-months** by summing (capital x time) over each period, then form the ratio.
A invests 6000 for 4 months, then adds 2000 (total 8000) for the next 8 months. A's capital-months = 6000x4 + 8000x8 = 24000 + 64000 = 88000. Use this against other partners' totals.
Break each partner's investment into periods of constant capital, weight each by its months, and add. The ratio of these sums is the profit ratio.

mcqs.explain: Each period's capital-months are summed to get the true weighting.

mcqs.explain: It's compound-partnership weighting applied piecewise across periods.

u:apt-31-si-basics.title: SI basics
u:apt-31-si-basics.summary: Simple interest is a flat rate on the original principal: SI = PRT/100.

blocks.text: **Simple Interest = (P x R x T)/100**, where P = principal, R = rate% per annum, T = time in years. The interest each year is the same (based only on the original principal). **Amount = P + SI.**
P=2000, R=5%, T=3: SI = 2000x5x3/100 = 300; amount = 2300. To find any variable, rearrange: R = SI x 100/(P x T), etc.
SI is linear in time — double the time, double the interest. Unlike compound interest, the base never grows, so it's always PRT/100.

u:apt-32-ci-annually-half-yearly-quarter.title: CI annually, half-yearly, quarterly
u:apt-32-ci-annually-half-yearly-quarter.summary: Compound interest grows on the accumulated amount; adjust rate and periods for compounding frequency.

blocks.text: **Amount = P x (1 + R/100)^T** (annual compounding). For **half-yearly**, use rate R/2 and 2T periods; for **quarterly**, R/4 and 4T periods. **CI = Amount - P.**
P=1000, R=10%, T=2 annually: A = 1000 x (1.1)^2 = 1210, CI = 210. Half-yearly at 10%: A = 1000 x (1.05)^4 = 1215.5 — more frequent compounding gives more interest.
More frequent compounding → higher effective yield. For n compoundings per year over T years: A = P(1 + R/(100n))^(nT).

u:apt-33-difference-between-ci-and-si-fo.title: Difference between CI and SI for 2 and 3 years
u:apt-33-difference-between-ci-and-si-fo.summary: Handy formulas: 2-year difference = P(R/100)^2; 3-year has an extra term.

blocks.text: The gap between compound and simple interest (same P, R, T) comes from interest-on-interest.

items: **2 years**: CI - SI = P x (R/100)^2.
**3 years**: CI - SI = P x (R/100)^2 x (3 + R/100), or equivalently P(R/100)^2 x (300+R)/100.

blocks.text: P=5000, R=10%, 2 years: difference = 5000 x (0.1)^2 = 50. These formulas let you find P or R directly from the given CI-SI difference.
The 2-year difference formula P(R/100)^2 is a favourite shortcut — it equals the simple interest on the first year's interest. Memorise it.

mcqs.explain: The 2-year difference is P times (R/100) squared.

u:apt-34-compound-growth-and-population.title: Compound growth and population
u:apt-34-compound-growth-and-population.summary: Population/value growing at a fixed rate follows the compound interest formula.

blocks.text: Anything growing at a fixed **percentage per period** compounds: **Final = Initial x (1 + r/100)^n.** For decline (depreciation), use (1 - r/100)^n.
Population 20000 growing 5%/year for 3 years: 20000 x (1.05)^3 = 23153. If growth rates differ per year, multiply the yearly factors: (1+r1)(1+r2)(1+r3).
This is compound interest under another name. Different yearly rates just mean multiplying different factors together — the same successive-change logic.

mcqs.explain: 10000 x 1.1 x 1.2 = 13200 (successive growth factors).

u:apt-35-instalments-and-emi-basics.title: Instalments and EMI basics
u:apt-35-instalments-and-emi-basics.summary: Equate the present values (or accumulated values) of instalments to the amount owed.

blocks.text: In **instalment** problems, a borrowed amount is repaid in equal parts, each earning/charged interest for its remaining time. The core idea: the **sum of the values of all instalments equals the debt** (with interest) at a common reference time.

For simple interest, bring each instalment to present value: an instalment paid after t years is worth (instalment) but 'covers' principal plus its interest. Set the total of instalments' present values equal to the borrowed sum and solve.
The technique is time-value equivalence: discount (or accumulate) each payment to a common point in time, then equate to the loan. EMI is the equal payment that makes this balance.

mcqs.q: The key principle in instalment problems is that:
options: The values of all instalments equal the debt at a common time
mcqs.explain: You equate the total time-adjusted value of payments to the amount owed.

mcqs.explain: Earlier payments are discounted less, so they carry more present value.

mcqs.q: EMI is the:
options: Equal periodic payment that repays the loan with interest
mcqs.explain: Equated Monthly Instalment is the constant payment amortising the loan.

u:apt-36-simple-average.title: Simple average
u:apt-36-simple-average.summary: Average = sum of values / number of values.

blocks.text: **Average (mean) = (sum of all values) / (number of values).** Equivalently, sum = average x count. Averages 'level out' a set of numbers.
If the average of 5 numbers is 20, their sum is 100. Adding a 6th number of 32 makes the new sum 132 and new average 22. Use sum = average x count to move between them.
The most useful rearrangement: total = average x count. Most average problems are solved by tracking the total.

u:apt-37-weighted-average.title: Weighted average
u:apt-37-weighted-average.summary: When groups have different sizes, weight each average by its count.

blocks.text: **Weighted average = (sum of value x weight) / (sum of weights).** When combining groups of different sizes, you can't just average the averages — weight by each group's count.
Class A: 20 students avg 60; Class B: 30 students avg 70. Combined = (20x60 + 30x70)/(20+30) = (1200+2100)/50 = 66 — closer to the larger group's average.
The combined average always lies between the two group averages, pulled toward the group with the larger weight. Simple-averaging the averages is wrong unless the weights are equal.

You must use a weighted average (not a simple one) when the groups have:

mcqs.explain: It's a weighted blend, so it falls between the two, nearer the larger group.

u:apt-38-average-of-consecutive-numbers.title: Average of consecutive numbers
u:apt-38-average-of-consecutive-numbers.summary: For evenly spaced numbers, the average is the middle term (or mean of the two middle terms).

blocks.text: For any set of **consecutive** (or evenly spaced) numbers, the average = **(first + last)/2** = the middle term. No need to sum everything.
Average of 1 to 100 = (1+100)/2 = 50.5. Average of first n natural numbers = (n+1)/2. Average of consecutive even/odd numbers also equals (first+last)/2.
Evenly spaced → symmetric → the mean is the midpoint. This shortcut avoids summing long sequences (and pairs with the sum formula n(n+1)/2).

mcqs.q: The average of the numbers 10, 11, 12, ..., 20 is:
mcqs.explain: (10+20)/2 = 15 (midpoint of an evenly spaced set).

mcqs.q: The average of the first n natural numbers is:
For evenly spaced numbers, the average equals:
mcqs.explain: Symmetry makes the mean the midpoint of the first and last terms.

u:apt-39-change-in-average-on-adding-rem.title: Change in average on adding/removing
u:apt-39-change-in-average-on-adding-rem.summary: Track the total: a new value shifts the average by (new value - old average)/new count.

blocks.text: When a value is added/removed, work with the **total**. New total = old total +/- the value; new average = new total / new count. Common in 'a new member changes the average' problems.
A team of 10 averages age 25 (total 250). A new member joins; average rises to 26 (11 members, total 286). New member's age = 286 - 250 = 36. Change in total = change in average x new count effect.
Always convert averages to totals, adjust the total, then recompute. The added value = new total - old total.

mcqs.q: 5 numbers average 20 (total 100). Adding a 6th makes the average 22. The 6th number is:
The reliable technique for add/remove average problems is to:
options: Convert to totals, adjust, then recompute
mcqs.explain: Working with totals correctly captures how one value shifts the mean.

mcqs.q: Removing a value equal to the current average leaves the average:
mcqs.explain: Removing an at-average value doesn't shift the mean.

u:apt-40-average-speed.title: Average speed
u:apt-40-average-speed.summary: Average speed = total distance / total time - not the simple mean of speeds.

blocks.text: **Average speed = total distance / total time.** For equal DISTANCES at speeds a and b, average speed = the **harmonic mean 2ab/(a+b)** — NOT (a+b)/2.
Go 60 km at 30 km/h (2h) and 60 km at 60 km/h (1h): avg = 120/3 = 40 km/h (harmonic mean = 2x30x60/90 = 40), not 45. Equal-distance trips use the harmonic mean.
The classic trap is averaging the two speeds. Use total distance / total time. For equal distances it's 2ab/(a+b); for equal times it IS the simple average (a+b)/2.

Average speed is defined as:
mcqs.explain: Average speed is always total distance divided by total time.

mcqs.q: For EQUAL TIMES at two speeds, the average speed is:
mcqs.explain: Equal times make the average the arithmetic mean; equal distances make it harmonic.

u:apt-41-alligation-rule.title: Alligation rule
u:apt-41-alligation-rule.summary: Find the ratio of two ingredients to hit a target mean by cross-differences.

blocks.text: The **rule of alligation** finds how to mix two things of different values to get a target mean value. **Ratio of cheaper : dearer = (dearer - mean) : (mean - cheaper).**
Mix rice at 20/kg and 30/kg to get a mean of 24/kg: ratio = (30-24):(24-20) = 6:4 = 3:2 (cheaper:dearer). The mean is closer to 20, so more cheaper rice.

Alligation applies to any weighted-average-in-reverse: prices, concentrations, speeds. Take the cross-differences from the mean; the ratio is inverse to the distances (the closer ingredient dominates).

mcqs.q: Mix milk at 12/L and 18/L to average 16/L. The ratio (12-milk : 18-milk) is:
By alligation, the mixing ratio is inversely related to each ingredient's:
mcqs.explain: The ingredient closer to the mean is used in greater proportion; ratio = cross-differences.

mcqs.q: Alligation is essentially reverse:
mcqs.explain: It finds the weights (ratio) that produce a given weighted-average mean.

u:apt-42-mixing-two-solutions.title: Mixing two solutions
u:apt-42-mixing-two-solutions.summary: Track the pure component; concentrations blend by weighted average (alligation).

blocks.text: When mixing two solutions of different concentrations, the resulting concentration is the **weighted average** of the two (by volume). Track the amount of the **pure component** (e.g. actual alcohol) to compute it.
Mix 4 L of 25% acid with 6 L of 50% acid: pure acid = 4x0.25 + 6x0.50 = 1 + 3 = 4 L in 10 L total = 40%. Or use alligation to find the mixing ratio for a target concentration.
Concentration of the mix = total pure component / total volume. Alligation gives the ratio directly if you know the target concentration.

mcqs.q: Mixing 3 L of 20% salt solution with 2 L of 45% gives what concentration?
The concentration of a mixture equals:
mcqs.explain: It's the pure component divided by the total volume — a weighted average.

mcqs.q: To reach a target concentration with two solutions, use:
mcqs.explain: Alligation gives the volume ratio needed to hit a target concentration.

u:apt-43-repeated-replacement-formula.title: Repeated replacement formula
u:apt-43-repeated-replacement-formula.summary: After removing and replacing x each time, remaining pure = P(1 - x/P)^n.

blocks.text: If from a container of volume P you repeatedly **remove x and replace with water**, after n operations the remaining original liquid = **P x (1 - x/P)^n**.
40 L of milk; remove 4 L and replace with water, done 2 times: milk left = 40 x (1 - 4/40)^2 = 40 x (0.9)^2 = 32.4 L. Each replacement multiplies the pure fraction by (1 - x/P).
The fraction of original remaining after n replacements is (1 - x/P)^n — the same compound-decay pattern. Memorise this formula for milk-and-water problems.

mcqs.q: From 50 L milk, 5 L is removed and replaced with water twice. Milk remaining:
The repeated-replacement formula for original liquid remaining is:
mcqs.explain: Each replacement scales the pure amount by (1 - x/P), applied n times.

mcqs.q: This formula follows the same pattern as:
mcqs.explain: Repeated multiplication by (1 - x/P) is compound decay.

u:apt-44-mixture-with-profit-loss-overla.title: Mixture with profit/loss overlap
u:apt-44-mixture-with-profit-loss-overla.summary: Combine mixture cost with a selling price to find profit - alligation plus profit%.

blocks.text: Some problems mix two goods at different costs (find the mixture's cost price via weighted average/alligation), then sell the blend at a price to compute **profit%** on that blended cost.
Mix 3 kg tea at 100 and 2 kg at 150: mixture CP per kg = (300+300)/5 = 120. Sold at 138/kg: profit% = (138-120)/120 x 100 = 15%.
Two steps: (1) find the mixture's cost price per unit (weighted average / alligation), (2) apply the profit/loss formula on that cost. Don't apply profit% to the individual ingredient prices.

u:apt-45-individual-and-combined-work-ra.title: Individual and combined work rate
u:apt-45-individual-and-combined-work-ra.summary: Work in terms of rates: if A takes a days and B takes b, together they take ab/(a+b).

blocks.text: Treat work as **rates** (fraction of job per day). If A finishes in a days, A's rate = 1/a. Combined rate = 1/a + 1/b, so together they take **ab/(a+b)** days.
A does a job in 10 days, B in 15: together = (10x15)/(10+15) = 150/25 = 6 days. For three workers, add all rates: 1/a + 1/b + 1/c, then invert.
Always convert 'days to finish' into 'rate = 1/days', add rates for combined work, then invert to get combined days. This handles any number of workers.

u:apt-46-work-with-efficiency-ratios.title: Work with efficiency ratios
u:apt-46-work-with-efficiency-ratios.summary: Efficiency is inversely proportional to time; use it to compare or combine workers.

blocks.text: **Efficiency is inversely proportional to time taken.** If A is twice as efficient as B, A takes half the time. Efficiency ratio = inverse of time ratio.
A is 3x as efficient as B; together they finish in 6 days. Their rates are 3k and k (total 4k). Since 4k finishes in 6 days, the job = 24k; A alone (3k) takes 8 days, B (k) takes 24 days.
Assign efficiencies (work/day), let total work = LCM or a convenient number, then compute times. Efficiency ratio a:b means time ratio b:a.

mcqs.explain: Efficiency and time are inverse; twice the efficiency means half the time (1:2).

mcqs.q: Efficiency is ______ proportional to time taken.
mcqs.explain: Higher efficiency means less time, so they are inversely proportional.

mcqs.explain: Time ratio is inverse 3:5; if A(eff 5)=6 days, work=30, B(eff 3)=30/3=10 days.

u:apt-47-men-days-hours-chain-rule.title: Men-days-hours (chain rule)
u:apt-47-men-days-hours-chain-rule.summary: M1 x D1 x H1 / W1 = M2 x D2 x H2 / W2 relates workers, days, hours, and work.

blocks.text: The **chain rule** (work equivalence): **(M1 x D1 x H1)/W1 = (M2 x D2 x H2)/W2**, where M = men, D = days, H = hours/day, W = work done. Solve for any unknown.
If 10 men build a wall in 8 days working 6 h/day, how many days for 12 men at 8 h/day (same wall)? 10x8x6 = 12xDx8 → D = 480/96 = 5 days.
Keep the total work (men x days x hours per unit of work) constant. More men or hours → fewer days. Include the work fraction W when the amount of work differs between scenarios.

mcqs.explain: 6x10 = 4xD, D = 60/4 = 15 days (inverse proportion).

options: Total work (men x days x hours per unit work)
mcqs.explain: Men x days x hours is proportional to work done, held equal across scenarios.

u:apt-48-pipes-and-cisterns-with-leaks.title: Pipes and cisterns with leaks
u:apt-48-pipes-and-cisterns-with-leaks.summary: Inlets add rate, outlets/leaks subtract - it's time-and-work with negative rates.

blocks.text: **Pipes and cisterns** is time-and-work with filling/emptying rates. An inlet filling in a hours has rate +1/a; a leak/outlet emptying in b hours has rate -1/b. Net rate = sum; time = 1/net rate.
Pipe fills in 6 h (+1/6), leak empties in 12 h (-1/12): net = 1/6 - 1/12 = 1/12, so it fills in 12 hours. If the leak is faster than the inlet, the tank never fills.
Treat outlets/leaks as negative work rates and add. If the net rate is positive, the tank fills; if negative or zero, it never does. Same rate-addition principle as time-and-work.

u:apt-49-alternate-day-working.title: Alternate day working
u:apt-49-alternate-day-working.summary: When workers alternate, sum work over a repeating cycle, then finish the remainder.

blocks.text: When workers **alternate days** (A works day 1, B day 2, ...), compute the work done in one **2-day cycle**, see how many full cycles fit, then handle the leftover work on the final day(s).

A does 1/10 per day, B does 1/15 per day, alternating starting with A. Per 2-day cycle: 1/10 + 1/15 = 1/6. After 5 cycles (10 days) = 5/6 done; A works day 11 doing 1/10, leaving 1/6 - 1/10... track carefully to the exact finishing day.
Cycle the combined rate, count complete cycles, then add partial days for the remainder. The starting worker matters for who finishes.

mcqs.explain: Summing a full cycle lets you count how many cycles fit before the remainder.

mcqs.q: A does 1/8/day, B does 1/8/day, alternating. One 2-day cycle completes:
mcqs.explain: 1/8 + 1/8 = 1/4 per 2-day cycle.

mcqs.q: In alternate-day problems, who finishes depends on:
options: Which worker starts and the leftover work
mcqs.explain: The remainder after full cycles is done by whoever's turn it is, set by the starter.

u:apt-50-wages-distribution.title: Wages distribution
u:apt-50-wages-distribution.summary: Wages split in the ratio of work done, i.e. in the ratio of efficiencies.

blocks.text: **Wages are distributed in the ratio of work done** (which equals the ratio of efficiencies for the same time, or 1/time for the same job). More efficient workers earn proportionally more.
A alone does a job in 6 days, B in 12 days. Their rates are 1/6 and 1/12, i.e. ratio 2:1. So total wages split 2:1 — A gets twice B's share. If total is 900, A gets 600, B gets 300.
Wage ratio = work ratio = efficiency ratio = inverse of time ratio (for the same job). Convert times to rates, form the ratio, and split the pay accordingly.

mcqs.q: A does a job in 4 days, B in 6 days. They share 500 wages in ratio:
Wages are distributed in the ratio of:
mcqs.explain: Pay is proportional to the work each contributes, i.e. their efficiency.

mcqs.q: For the same job, the wage ratio is the ______ of the time ratio.
mcqs.explain: Faster (less time) means more work, so wage ratio is inverse to time ratio.

u:apt-51-train-crossing-pole-platform.title: Train crossing pole/platform
u:apt-51-train-crossing-pole-platform.summary: Crossing a pole covers the train's length; crossing a platform covers length + platform.

blocks.text: A train crossing a **pole/man** (a point) travels a distance equal to its **own length**. Crossing a **platform/bridge** travels **train length + platform length**. Time = distance / speed.
A 200 m train at 20 m/s crosses a pole in 200/20 = 10 s. To cross a 100 m platform: (200+100)/20 = 15 s. Convert km/h to m/s by multiplying by 5/18.
Always ask: what distance is covered? A point (pole/man) → train length only. A length (platform/tunnel/another train) → sum of both lengths. Keep units consistent (m/s).

mcqs.q: A 150 m train at 15 m/s crosses a pole in:
mcqs.explain: Distance = train length 150 m; time = 150/15 = 10 s.

mcqs.q: Crossing a platform, the distance a train covers is:
mcqs.explain: The full train must clear the platform, so distance = both lengths.

mcqs.q: To convert 72 km/h to m/s, multiply by:
mcqs.explain: km/h to m/s uses factor 5/18: 72 x 5/18 = 20 m/s.

u:apt-52-two-trains-same-and-opposite-di.title: Two trains same and opposite direction
u:apt-52-two-trains-same-and-opposite-di.summary: Add speeds when trains move toward each other, subtract when moving the same way.

blocks.text: When two trains cross each other, the distance covered = **sum of their lengths**, at the **relative speed**. Opposite directions: relative speed = **sum** of speeds. Same direction: relative speed = **difference**.
Two trains 120 m and 80 m, speeds 15 and 10 m/s, opposite: relative speed = 25 m/s, distance = 200 m, time = 8 s. Same direction: relative speed = 5 m/s, time = 40 s (much longer).
Opposite → add speeds (they approach fast); same direction → subtract (the faster overtakes slowly). Distance is always the sum of both train lengths when they fully pass each other.

mcqs.q: Two trains moving in opposite directions cross at a relative speed equal to:
mcqs.explain: Opposite directions add speeds, so they pass quickly.

mcqs.q: When one train overtakes another (same direction), relative speed is the:
mcqs.explain: Same direction subtracts speeds; the faster gains on the slower slowly.

mcqs.q: The distance for two trains to completely cross each other is:
mcqs.explain: Both trains must fully pass, so distance = length1 + length2.

u:apt-53-upstream-and-downstream.title: Upstream and downstream
u:apt-53-upstream-and-downstream.summary: Downstream speed = boat + stream; upstream = boat - stream.

blocks.text: For a boat in a river: **Downstream speed = boat speed + stream speed** (current helps). **Upstream speed = boat speed - stream speed** (current opposes). Distance = speed x time as usual.
Boat 10 km/h, stream 2 km/h: downstream = 12, upstream = 8. To go 24 km downstream: 24/12 = 2 h; upstream: 24/8 = 3 h. The current adds to speed one way and subtracts the other.
Downstream = b + s, upstream = b - s. From these two, boat speed = (down + up)/2 and stream speed = (down - up)/2.

mcqs.q: Boat speed 8 km/h, stream 3 km/h. Downstream speed is:
mcqs.explain: Downstream = boat + stream = 8 + 3 = 11 km/h.

mcqs.q: Upstream speed equals:
mcqs.explain: Going against the current, the stream speed subtracts.

mcqs.q: If downstream = 14 and upstream = 6 km/h, the stream speed is:
mcqs.explain: Stream = (down - up)/2 = (14-6)/2 = 4 km/h.

u:apt-54-still-water-speed.title: Still water speed
u:apt-54-still-water-speed.summary: Boat speed in still water = (downstream + upstream)/2.

blocks.text: The boat's **speed in still water** = **(downstream speed + upstream speed)/2**, and the **stream speed** = (downstream - upstream)/2. These invert the upstream/downstream relations.
Given downstream 16 km/h and upstream 10 km/h: boat = (16+10)/2 = 13 km/h, stream = (16-10)/2 = 3 km/h. If a boat covers d km up in tu and down in td, you can back out both speeds.
Still-water speed is the AVERAGE of downstream and upstream speeds; stream speed is HALF their difference. These two formulas unlock most boats-and-streams questions.

mcqs.q: Downstream 18 km/h, upstream 12 km/h. Still-water boat speed is:
Still-water speed is the ______ of downstream and upstream speeds.
mcqs.explain: Boat speed = (downstream + upstream)/2.

mcqs.q: The stream speed equals:
mcqs.explain: Stream = half the difference of downstream and upstream speeds.

u:apt-55-average-speed-round-trip.title: Average speed round trip
u:apt-55-average-speed-round-trip.summary: For equal distances at speeds a and b, average = 2ab/(a+b), the harmonic mean.

blocks.text: A round trip covers the **same distance** each way. If going speed = a and returning speed = b, average speed = **2ab/(a+b)** (harmonic mean) — never the simple average.
Go at 40 km/h, return at 60 km/h: average = 2x40x60/(40+60) = 4800/100 = 48 km/h (not 50). The slower leg takes more time, dragging the average below the midpoint.
Equal distance → harmonic mean 2ab/(a+b). This appears in boats (up/down same distance), commuting, and any there-and-back scenario. Averaging the speeds is the classic wrong answer.

mcqs.q: A trip out at 30 km/h and back at 20 km/h has average speed:
For equal-distance round trips, the average speed is the:
mcqs.explain: Equal distances weight time toward the slower leg, giving the harmonic mean.

mcqs.q: Why is the round-trip average less than the simple mean of speeds?
options: The slower leg takes more time, lowering the average
mcqs.explain: More time is spent at the slower speed, pulling the average down.

u:apt-56-basic-tsd.title: Basic TSD
u:apt-56-basic-tsd.summary: Distance = Speed x Time - the triangle from which everything follows.

blocks.text: **Distance = Speed x Time.** Rearrange: Speed = Distance/Time, Time = Distance/Speed. Keep units consistent (km & h, or m & s). Convert km/h to m/s with x 5/18, and m/s to km/h with x 18/5.
A car at 60 km/h for 2.5 h covers 150 km. If speed is constant, distance is proportional to time; if distance is fixed, speed and time are inversely proportional.
Master the unit conversions (5/18 and 18/5) and the D = S x T triangle. Every speed problem is a rearrangement of this.

mcqs.q: A train travels 240 km in 4 hours. Its speed is:
mcqs.explain: Speed = distance/time = 240/4 = 60 km/h.

mcqs.q: To convert 90 km/h to m/s, multiply by:
For a fixed distance, speed and time are:
mcqs.explain: D = S x T constant means higher speed gives lower time.

u:apt-57-relative-speed.title: Relative speed
u:apt-57-relative-speed.summary: Add speeds for opposite directions, subtract for same direction.

blocks.text: **Relative speed** is how fast one object approaches/recedes from another. **Opposite directions: add** the speeds. **Same direction: subtract** them. The gap closes at the relative speed.
Two people 100 m apart walk toward each other at 3 and 2 m/s: they meet in 100/(3+2) = 20 s. If chasing (same direction) at 5 and 3 m/s with a 40 m lead: caught in 40/(5-3) = 20 s.
Time to meet/catch = gap / relative speed. Opposite → sum (fast closing); same direction → difference (slow closing). This underlies trains, races, and chase problems.

mcqs.q: Two cars approach each other at 40 and 60 km/h. Their relative speed is:
mcqs.explain: Opposite directions add: 40 + 60 = 100 km/h.

mcqs.q: A faster runner chasing a slower one closes the gap at a speed equal to the:
mcqs.explain: Same direction: relative speed is the difference.

mcqs.q: Time to meet equals:
mcqs.explain: The gap divided by the relative closing speed gives the meeting time.

u:apt-58-average-speed-harmonic-mean-cas.title: Average speed (harmonic mean cases)
u:apt-58-average-speed-harmonic-mean-cas.summary: Equal distances give the harmonic mean; equal times give the arithmetic mean.

blocks.text: Average speed = total distance / total time. The shortcut depends on what's equal.
Same distance at 20 and 30: 2x20x30/50 = 24 (harmonic). Same time at 20 and 30: (20+30)/2 = 25 (arithmetic). Identify which is equal before choosing the mean.
Equal distance → harmonic; equal time → arithmetic. When neither is equal, fall back to total distance / total time explicitly.

mcqs.q: For equal distances at 10 and 40 km/h, the average speed is:
mcqs.explain: Harmonic mean = 2x10x40/50 = 800/50 = 16 km/h.

mcqs.q: For equal TIMES at two speeds, the average speed is the:
mcqs.explain: Equal times make it the simple arithmetic average.

mcqs.q: The general definition of average speed is:
mcqs.explain: It's always total distance over total time; the means are special-case shortcuts.

u:apt-59-races-and-head-starts.title: Races and head starts
u:apt-59-races-and-head-starts.summary: 'A beats B by x metres or t seconds' relates their speeds via equal time or distance.

blocks.text: In races, phrases like 'A gives B a start of x m' or 'A beats B by t seconds' encode speed ratios. When A finishes, compare how far/behind B is at the same TIME, or the time gap at the same DISTANCE.
'A beats B by 20 m in a 100 m race' means when A runs 100 m, B runs 80 m — so speed ratio A:B = 100:80 = 5:4. A 'start of 20 m' means B only needs to run 80 m.
'Beats by distance' → compare distances at equal time (gives the speed ratio). 'Beats by time' → compare times at equal distance. A head start reduces the distance the slower runner must cover.

mcqs.q: In a 100 m race, A beats B by 25 m. The speed ratio A:B is:
mcqs.explain: When A runs 100, B runs 75, so ratio = 100:75 = 4:3.

mcqs.q: 'A gives B a 10 m start in a 100 m race' means B runs:
mcqs.explain: B starts 10 m ahead, so B only covers 90 m to finish.

mcqs.q: 'A beats B by t seconds' is compared at equal:
mcqs.explain: A time gap is measured over the same race distance.

u:apt-60-circular-track-meetings.title: Circular track meetings
u:apt-60-circular-track-meetings.summary: On a circular track, meeting times depend on relative speed and track length.

blocks.text: Two runners on a **circular track** of length L: time to meet = L / relative speed. **Opposite directions**: relative speed = sum; **same direction**: difference.

items: **First meeting**: opposite → L/(a+b); same direction → L/(a-b).
**Meeting at the START point**: time = LCM of each runner's lap time (L/a and L/b).

blocks.text: Track 400 m; speeds 8 and 5 m/s, same direction: first meeting in 400/(8-5) = 133.3 s. Meeting at the start = LCM(400/8, 400/5) = LCM(50, 80) = 400 s.
Distinguish 'meet anywhere' (relative speed, L/(sum or diff)) from 'meet at the starting point' (LCM of lap times). Opposite direction meetings are more frequent (higher relative speed).

mcqs.q: On a 300 m track, two runners at 6 and 4 m/s in opposite directions first meet after:
mcqs.explain: Opposite: relative speed 10 m/s, time = 300/10 = 30 s.

mcqs.q: Runners meeting again at the STARTING point occurs at time:
options: LCM of their individual lap times
mcqs.explain: Both must complete whole laps simultaneously, given by the LCM of lap times.

mcqs.q: Same-direction meetings on a circular track use relative speed equal to the:
mcqs.explain: Same direction subtracts speeds, so they meet less often than in opposite directions.

u:apt-61-present-past-future-age-equatio.title: Present, past, future age equations
u:apt-61-present-past-future-age-equatio.summary: Add or subtract the same number of years to every person's age; then set up equations.

blocks.text: Let present ages be variables. **t years ago**: subtract t from each; **t years hence**: add t to each. Translate the word conditions into equations and solve.
'A is 4 years older than B' → A = B + 4. '5 years ago A was twice B' → (A-5) = 2(B-5). Solve simultaneously. The same t is added/subtracted to everyone — a common slip is changing only one age.
Everyone ages by the same amount over the same period. Set present ages as variables, shift all by t for past/future, and form equations from the statements.

mcqs.q: A is 3 times as old as B, and A is 24 more than B. B's age is:
't years ago' means each person's age is:
mcqs.explain: Going back t years subtracts t from every current age.

mcqs.q: A common mistake in age problems is:
options: Changing only one person's age for a past/future shift
mcqs.explain: All ages shift by the same t; changing only one is the classic error.

u:apt-62-ratio-based-age-problems.title: Ratio-based age problems
u:apt-62-ratio-based-age-problems.summary: Express ages as multiples of x, then apply the time condition.

blocks.text: When ages are given as a ratio, let them be **kx** for the ratio terms. Use the second condition (a sum, or a ratio at a different time) to solve for x, then compute actual ages.
Present ages ratio 4:5; in 6 years the ratio becomes 5:6. Let ages be 4x, 5x. Then (4x+6)/(5x+6) = 5/6 → cross-multiply → 24x+36 = 25x+30 → x = 6. Ages: 24 and 30.
Ratio ages → write as 4x, 5x. Then impose the time-shifted ratio and solve for x. This turns the word problem into one linear equation.

mcqs.q: Present ages are in ratio 3:4; sum is 42. The younger age is:
mcqs.explain: 3x + 4x = 42 → x = 6; younger = 18.

mcqs.q: The first step for ratio age problems is to write ages as:
mcqs.explain: Expressing the ratio as 3x, 4x lets the extra condition solve for x.

mcqs.q: Ages ratio 5:7 now; difference is 10 years. The elder is:
mcqs.explain: Difference 2x = 10 → x = 5; elder = 7x = 35.

u:apt-63-average-age-of-a-group.title: Average age of a group
u:apt-63-average-age-of-a-group.summary: Group age problems use total age = average x number of people.

blocks.text: **Total age = average age x number of people.** When someone joins/leaves or is replaced, work with totals. A common type: a member is replaced and the average changes — the difference reveals the age gap.
A team of 11 averages 25 (total 275). When a 36-year-old replaces someone, average rises by 1 (to 26, total 286). Age difference = 286 - 275 = 11, so the replaced person was 36 - 11 = 25.
Change in total = change in average x number of people. Replacement problems: (new person - old person) = (change in average) x group size.

mcqs.q: A class of 20 averages age 15. The total age is:
mcqs.explain: Total = average x count = 15 x 20 = 300.

mcqs.q: When one member is replaced, the change in total age equals:
mcqs.explain: Only the swapped member changes the total, by the difference of their ages.

mcqs.q: If replacing a member raises a 10-person average by 2, the new member is older than the old by:
mcqs.explain: Change in total = 2 x 10 = 20, so the new member is 20 years older.

blocks.text: For 11: subtract and add digits alternately (from right); if the result is 0 or a multiple of 11, it's divisible. e.g. 918082: 2-8+0-8+1-9 = -22, divisible by 11.
For composite divisors, combine coprime factors: divisible by 12 = divisible by 3 AND 4; by 15 = by 3 AND 5. Digit-sum rules (3, 9) and last-digits rules (4, 8) are the workhorses.

mcqs.q: A number is divisible by 9 if:
options: Its digit sum is divisible by 9
mcqs.explain: The digit-sum rule: divisibility by 9 iff the sum of digits is divisible by 9.

mcqs.q: Divisibility by 4 is tested using the:
mcqs.explain: A number is divisible by 4 iff its last two digits form a multiple of 4.

mcqs.q: To check divisibility by 12, verify divisibility by:
mcqs.explain: 12 = 3 x 4 (coprime), so check both 3 and 4.

u:apt-65-unit-digit-and-cyclicity.title: Unit digit and cyclicity
u:apt-65-unit-digit-and-cyclicity.summary: The last digit of a power cycles with period dividing 4; use the exponent mod 4.

blocks.text: The **unit (last) digit** of a^n repeats in a cycle. For most digits the cycle length divides 4, so reduce the **exponent modulo 4** to find the last digit.
Last digit of 7^102: cycle 7,9,3,1; 102 mod 4 = 2, so it's the 2nd term = 9. If the remainder is 0, use the LAST digit of the cycle.
Reduce the exponent mod 4 (mod cycle length), then read the corresponding digit. Digits 0,1,5,6 always end in themselves; 4 and 9 have 2-cycles.

mcqs.q: The unit digit of 2^10 is:
mcqs.explain: Cycle 2,4,8,6; 10 mod 4 = 2, so the 2nd term = 4.

mcqs.q: The unit digit of any power of 5 is:
mcqs.explain: 5 raised to any positive power always ends in 5.

mcqs.q: To find the unit digit of a^n, reduce n modulo:
mcqs.explain: The last digit repeats with the base's cycle length, usually 4.

u:apt-66-remainder-theorem-basics.title: Remainder theorem basics
u:apt-66-remainder-theorem-basics.summary: Reduce each factor mod n, then combine - and use negative remainders to simplify.

blocks.text: To find a remainder, work with **modular arithmetic**: (a x b) mod n = [(a mod n) x (b mod n)] mod n, and similarly for sums. Reduce big numbers to their remainders first.
Use NEGATIVE remainders to simplify: 17 mod 6 = -1 (since 17 = 18 - 1). So 17^20 mod 6 = (-1)^20 = 1. And Fermat: if p is prime and a not divisible by p, a^(p-1) mod p = 1.
Reduce each part modulo n before multiplying/adding, and prefer the smaller (possibly negative) remainder. For powers, look for a base congruent to 1 or -1 mod n, which collapses the exponent.

mcqs.q: The remainder when 7^100 is divided by 6 is:
In modular arithmetic, (a x b) mod n equals:
options: [(a mod n)(b mod n)] mod n
mcqs.explain: You can reduce each factor mod n before multiplying.

mcqs.q: 17 mod 6 can be written as which negative remainder?
mcqs.explain: 17 = 18 - 1, so 17 is congruent to -1 (mod 6), useful for powers.

u:apt-67-number-of-factors.title: Number of factors
u:apt-67-number-of-factors.summary: From prime factorisation p^a x q^b, the number of factors is (a+1)(b+1)...

blocks.text: Prime-factorise N = p^a x q^b x r^c ... Then the **number of factors (divisors) = (a+1)(b+1)(c+1)...** Each prime's exponent can independently be 0 to its power.
72 = 2^3 x 3^2, so factors = (3+1)(2+1) = 12. The number of EVEN factors of 72 = subtract those with no 2: total 12 minus odd factors (3^2 → (2+1)=3) = 9 even factors.
Number of factors = product of (each exponent + 1). For only even/odd factors, split off the factor of 2. A perfect square has an ODD number of factors (all exponents even + 1 is odd).

mcqs.q: How many factors does 36 (= 2^2 x 3^2) have?
The number of factors of p^a x q^b is:
mcqs.explain: Each exponent ranges 0..its power, giving (a+1)(b+1) combinations.

mcqs.q: A number has an odd number of factors if and only if it is a:
mcqs.explain: Only perfect squares have a divisor pairing with itself, making the count odd.

u:apt-68-sum-of-factors.title: Sum of factors
u:apt-68-sum-of-factors.summary: Sum of divisors = product of (p^(a+1)-1)/(p-1) over each prime power.

blocks.text: For N = p^a x q^b ..., the **sum of all factors** = [ (p^(a+1)-1)/(p-1) ] x [ (q^(b+1)-1)/(q-1) ] x ... Each bracket is the geometric-series sum of that prime's powers (1 + p + p^2 + ... + p^a).
12 = 2^2 x 3: sum = (1+2+4)(1+3) = 7 x 4 = 28 (indeed 1+2+3+4+6+12 = 28). Each factor of the product covers all powers of one prime.
Sum of factors multiplies the geometric-series sums of each prime's powers. It's the same multiplicative structure as the count of factors, but summing instead of counting.

mcqs.q: The sum of factors of 12 is:
For each prime power p^a, its contribution to the factor sum is:
mcqs.explain: It's the geometric-series sum of all powers of p up to p^a.

mcqs.q: The sum of factors is a ______ function of the prime powers.
mcqs.explain: Multiply the per-prime geometric sums to get the total.

u:apt-69-last-two-digits.title: Last two digits
u:apt-69-last-two-digits.summary: Find a number mod 100 - patterns for numbers ending in 1 and powers of 2 help.

blocks.text: The **last two digits** of a number are the number mod 100. Some useful patterns:

items: **Ends in 1** (like 31^n): last two digits = (last digit of tens-digit x n) followed by 1. e.g. 31^7: tens = 3x7 = 21 → last two digits ...1 → 11.
**Powers of 2**: last two digits cycle with period 20 after 2^2. Know 2^10 = ...24, 2^20 = ...76.
General: use mod 100 arithmetic, reducing at each step.

blocks.text: For numbers ending in 1: last two digits of (a1)^n = [(a x n) mod 10]1. e.g. 71^13: 7x13 = 91 → tens digit 1 → last two digits 11.
Last two digits = value mod 100. Learn the shortcut for '...1' bases and the cycle for powers of 2; otherwise reduce mod 100 repeatedly.

mcqs.q: The last two digits of 31^4 are:
mcqs.explain: For a base ending in 1, tens digit = (3 x 4) mod 10 = 2, so the last two digits are 21.

mcqs.q: The last two digits of a number equal the number modulo:
mcqs.explain: Mod 100 isolates the final two digits.

mcqs.q: For a base ending in 1, the tens digit of the power depends on:
mcqs.explain: The pattern for '...1' bases uses (tens x n) mod 10 as the new tens digit.

u:apt-70-base-system-conversion.title: Base system conversion
u:apt-70-base-system-conversion.summary: Convert to decimal by positional weights; convert from decimal by repeated division.

blocks.text: In base b, each digit's value is digit x b^position. **To decimal**: sum digit x b^i. **From decimal**: repeatedly divide by b, reading remainders bottom-up.
Binary 1011 to decimal = 1x8 + 0x4 + 1x2 + 1x1 = 11. Decimal 13 to binary: 13/2=6 r1, 6/2=3 r0, 3/2=1 r1, 1/2=0 r1 → read up: 1101.
To decimal: weighted sum of digits by powers of the base. From decimal: successive division by the base, remainders give digits (least significant first). Base 16 (hex) uses A-F for 10-15.

mcqs.q: Binary 1101 in decimal is:
To convert a decimal number to base b, you:
options: Repeatedly divide by b and read remainders
mcqs.explain: Successive division by b gives the digits (from least significant).

mcqs.q: In hexadecimal, the digit 'C' represents:
mcqs.explain: Hex A-F represent 10-15, so C = 12.

u:apt-71-hcf-lcm-computation.title: HCF/LCM computation
u:apt-71-hcf-lcm-computation.summary: HCF is the product of common primes (lowest powers); LCM uses all primes (highest powers).

blocks.text: From prime factorisations: **HCF (GCD)** = product of common prime factors with the **lowest** powers. **LCM** = product of all prime factors with the **highest** powers.
12 = 2^2 x 3, 18 = 2 x 3^2. HCF = 2^1 x 3^1 = 6 (lowest powers). LCM = 2^2 x 3^2 = 36 (highest powers). Euclid's algorithm also finds HCF fast: HCF(a,b) = HCF(b, a mod b).
HCF = LOW powers of COMMON primes; LCM = HIGH powers of ALL primes. HCF divides both numbers; LCM is a multiple of both.

mcqs.q: The HCF of 24 and 36 is:
The LCM of 4 and 6 is:
HCF is formed using the ______ powers of ______ primes.
mcqs.explain: HCF uses the lowest powers of the primes common to all numbers.

blocks.text: **LCM of fractions = LCM(numerators) / HCF(denominators).** **HCF of fractions = HCF(numerators) / LCM(denominators).** (Fractions in lowest terms.)
Swap the roles for fractions: LCM uses LCM-of-tops over HCF-of-bottoms; HCF uses HCF-of-tops over LCM-of-bottoms. Reduce fractions first.

mcqs.q: The LCM of 1/2 and 3/4 is:
LCM of fractions equals:
mcqs.explain: LCM of numerators over HCF of denominators.

mcqs.q: The HCF of 2/3 and 4/5 is:

u:apt-73-word-problems-bells-lights-tile.title: Word problems: bells, lights, tiles
u:apt-73-word-problems-bells-lights-tile.summary: 'Together again' uses LCM; 'largest equal size' uses HCF.

blocks.text: Classic HCF/LCM word problems. **LCM** answers 'when do events coincide/recur together?' (bells tolling, lights flashing). **HCF** answers 'largest equal-sized pieces?' (tiles, rope lengths, distributing evenly).
Bells ring every 6, 8, 12 s: together again after LCM(6,8,12) = 24 s. Largest square tile for a 6m x 8m floor: HCF(600, 800) = 200 cm. 'Same time again' → LCM; 'greatest common size' → HCF.
Keyword map: 'meet/ring/happen together' → LCM; 'largest/maximum equal / exactly divide' → HCF. Identifying which is being asked is the whole skill.

mcqs.q: Three lights flash every 4, 6, and 10 seconds. They flash together every:
'Largest tile to exactly cover a floor' is found using:
mcqs.explain: The greatest common measure that divides both dimensions is the HCF.

mcqs.q: Events recurring 'together again' are timed by their:
mcqs.explain: The LCM is the first common multiple where all cycles align.

u:apt-74-hcf-lcm-product-relation.title: HCF-LCM product relation
u:apt-74-hcf-lcm-product-relation.summary: For two numbers, HCF x LCM = product of the numbers.

blocks.text: For any two numbers a and b: **HCF(a,b) x LCM(a,b) = a x b.** This lets you find one quantity when the other three are known. (It holds only for TWO numbers, not three or more.)
If two numbers have HCF 6 and LCM 36, and one is 12, the other = (6 x 36)/12 = 18. Also, LCM is always a multiple of HCF, and both numbers are multiples of the HCF.
HCF x LCM = product (for two numbers only). If numbers are HCF x m and HCF x n with m,n coprime, then LCM = HCF x m x n.

mcqs.q: Two numbers have HCF 4 and LCM 48. If one is 16, the other is:
For two numbers, HCF x LCM equals:
mcqs.explain: HCF x LCM = a x b holds for exactly two numbers.

mcqs.q: The LCM of two numbers is always a:
mcqs.explain: The LCM is a multiple of the HCF (and of both numbers).

u:apt-75-lines-and-angles.title: Lines and angles
u:apt-75-lines-and-angles.summary: Angle relationships on lines and with parallels: supplementary, vertical, and transversal angles.

items: Angles on a straight line sum to **180 degrees** (linear pair / supplementary).
**Vertically opposite** angles (formed by two crossing lines) are equal.
With a transversal cutting **parallel lines**: corresponding angles equal, alternate angles equal, co-interior (same-side) angles sum to 180.
Angles around a point sum to **360 degrees**.

blocks.text: The three workhorses: straight line = 180, vertically opposite = equal, and the parallel-line angle rules (corresponding/alternate equal, co-interior supplementary). Most angle-chasing reduces to these.

mcqs.q: Two angles forming a linear pair (on a straight line) sum to:
mcqs.explain: Angles on a straight line are supplementary, summing to 180 degrees.

mcqs.q: Vertically opposite angles are:
mcqs.explain: When two lines cross, the opposite angles are equal.

mcqs.q: Co-interior (same-side) angles between parallel lines sum to:
mcqs.explain: Same-side interior angles are supplementary (sum 180) for parallel lines.

u:apt-76-triangle-properties-and-similar.title: Triangle properties and similarity
u:apt-76-triangle-properties-and-similar.summary: Angle sum 180, exterior-angle rule, and similar triangles with proportional sides.

items: Angles of a triangle sum to **180 degrees**.
**Exterior angle** = sum of the two opposite interior angles.
**Similar triangles** (equal angles) have **proportional sides**; ratio of areas = (ratio of sides)^2.
**Congruent** triangles are identical (SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS).

blocks.text: If two triangles are similar with side ratio 2:3, their areas are in ratio 4:9 (square the side ratio). Use similarity to find unknown sides via proportions.
Similar → same shape, proportional sides, area ratio = side ratio squared. The angle-sum (180) and exterior-angle rules unlock most angle problems; similarity handles side-length problems.

mcqs.q: The angles of any triangle sum to:
mcqs.explain: Every triangle's interior angles total 180 degrees.

mcqs.q: Two similar triangles have sides in ratio 3:5. Their areas are in ratio:
mcqs.explain: Area ratio is the square of the side ratio: 9:25.

mcqs.q: An exterior angle of a triangle equals:
options: The sum of the two opposite interior angles
mcqs.explain: The exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles.

u:apt-77-pythagorean-triples.title: Pythagorean triples
u:apt-77-pythagorean-triples.summary: Right triangles satisfy a^2 + b^2 = c^2; memorise common triples to save time.

blocks.text: For a right triangle, **hypotenuse^2 = sum of the squares of the other two sides** (a^2 + b^2 = c^2). Recognising common **Pythagorean triples** avoids calculation.
Spot the triples and their multiples instantly. If two sides are 6 and 8, the hypotenuse is 10 (a 3-4-5 scaled by 2) — no square-root needed. These recur throughout geometry and mensuration.

mcqs.q: A right triangle has legs 9 and 12. Its hypotenuse is:
mcqs.explain: 9-12-15 is a 3-4-5 triple scaled by 3, so hypotenuse = 15.

mcqs.q: Which is a Pythagorean triple?
The Pythagorean theorem relates the hypotenuse c to legs a, b by:
mcqs.explain: In a right triangle, the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the legs.

u:apt-78-circles-chords-tangents.title: Circles: chords, tangents
u:apt-78-circles-chords-tangents.summary: Key circle theorems for chords, tangents, and angles subtended.

items: **Circumference = 2*pi*r; Area = pi*r^2.**
A **tangent** is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.
Tangents drawn from an external point are **equal** in length.
The angle at the **centre** is twice the angle at the circumference on the same arc.
Angle in a **semicircle** is 90 degrees.

blocks.text: The perpendicular from the centre bisects a chord. Equal chords are equidistant from the centre. These help find chord lengths and distances quickly.
Tangent-perpendicular-to-radius and 'angle at centre = 2 x angle at circumference' are the two most-used circle theorems. Angle in a semicircle = 90 is a frequent shortcut.

mcqs.q: A tangent to a circle is ______ to the radius at the point of contact.
mcqs.explain: The tangent meets the radius at 90 degrees at the contact point.

mcqs.q: The angle in a semicircle is:
mcqs.explain: An angle subtended by a diameter at the circumference is a right angle.

mcqs.q: The angle subtended by an arc at the centre versus at the circumference is:
mcqs.explain: The central angle is twice the inscribed angle on the same arc.

u:apt-79-coordinate-geometry-basics.title: Coordinate geometry basics
u:apt-79-coordinate-geometry-basics.summary: Distance, midpoint, slope, and the section formula for points in the plane.

items: **Distance** between (x1,y1) and (x2,y2) = sqrt[(x2-x1)^2 + (y2-y1)^2].
**Slope** = (y2-y1)/(x2-x1). Parallel lines have equal slopes; perpendicular lines have slopes multiplying to -1.
**Section formula** (dividing in ratio m:n): ((mx2+nx1)/(m+n), (my2+ny1)/(m+n)).

blocks.text: Distance uses Pythagoras on the coordinate differences; midpoint averages the coordinates. Slope captures direction: equal for parallel, product -1 for perpendicular lines.

mcqs.q: The distance between (0,0) and (3,4) is:
The midpoint of (2,6) and (8,10) is:
Two perpendicular lines have slopes whose product is:
mcqs.explain: Perpendicular lines satisfy m1 x m2 = -1; parallel lines have equal slopes.

u:apt-80-2d-areas-and-perimeters.title: 2D areas and perimeters
u:apt-80-2d-areas-and-perimeters.summary: Formulas for areas and perimeters of common plane figures.

blocks.text: For an equilateral triangle of side a: area = (sqrt3/4) a^2. Heron's formula for any triangle: area = sqrt[s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)] where s = (a+b+c)/2.
Memorise these; most mensuration problems combine them. The circle (pi*r^2) and triangle (1/2 base x height) appear most often.

mcqs.q: The area of a triangle with base 10 and height 6 is:
The area of a circle of radius 7 (pi = 22/7) is:
The perimeter of a square of side 9 is:
mcqs.explain: Perimeter = 4 x side = 36.

u:apt-81-3d-volumes-and-surface-areas.title: 3D volumes and surface areas
u:apt-81-3d-volumes-and-surface-areas.summary: Volume and surface-area formulas for cuboids, cubes, and prisms.

blocks.text: Cube diagonal = a*sqrt3; cuboid diagonal = sqrt(l^2+b^2+h^2). Cone slant height l = sqrt(r^2 + h^2). Curved (lateral) surface area of a cylinder = 2*pi*r*h.
Distinguish TOTAL surface area (includes bases) from CURVED/lateral surface area (sides only). Volume scales with the cube of linear size; surface area with the square.

mcqs.q: The volume of a cube of side 5 is:
The total surface area of a cube of side 4 is:
The volume of a sphere is:
mcqs.explain: Sphere volume = (4/3)pi r^3; its surface area is 4*pi*r^2.

u:apt-82-cylinder-cone-sphere.title: Cylinder, cone, sphere
u:apt-82-cylinder-cone-sphere.summary: The round solids and the neat relationships between their volumes.

items: **Cylinder**: V = pi*r^2*h; curved SA = 2*pi*r*h; total SA = 2*pi*r(r+h).
**Cone**: V = (1/3)pi*r^2*h; curved SA = pi*r*l (l = slant); total SA = pi*r(r+l).
**Sphere**: V = (4/3)pi*r^3; SA = 4*pi*r^2; **hemisphere** V = (2/3)pi*r^3.

blocks.text: A cone has exactly 1/3 the volume of a cylinder with the same base and height. A sphere's volume = 2/3 of the cylinder that just contains it. These ratios are frequently tested.
Remember the 1/3 factor for cones (vs cylinders) and l = sqrt(r^2 + h^2) for slant height. Curved surface area excludes the base(s); total includes them.

mcqs.q: A cone and a cylinder have the same base and height. The cone's volume is what fraction of the cylinder's?
mcqs.explain: Cone volume = (1/3)pi r^2 h, exactly one-third of the cylinder.

mcqs.q: The slant height l of a cone with radius r and height h is:
mcqs.explain: The slant is the hypotenuse: l = sqrt(r^2 + h^2).

mcqs.q: The curved surface area of a cylinder is:
mcqs.explain: The lateral (curved) surface area is 2*pi*r*h, excluding the two circular bases.

u:apt-83-combination-solids.title: Combination solids
u:apt-83-combination-solids.summary: Add or subtract component volumes/areas for composite shapes.

blocks.text: **Combination (composite) solids** are made of basic solids joined together (e.g. a cone on a cylinder, a hemisphere on a cone). Compute by **adding** the parts' volumes, and for surface area, adding only the EXPOSED surfaces (not the joined faces).
An ice-cream shape (cone + hemisphere on top): volume = cone + hemisphere. Surface area = cone's curved SA + hemisphere's curved SA (the flat circular join is internal, so exclude it).
Volumes always add. For surface area, count only the OUTER exposed faces — the surfaces where two solids join are hidden. Melting/recasting problems conserve volume (equate before and after).

mcqs.q: For a solid made of a cone atop a cylinder, the total volume is:
mcqs.explain: Component volumes add for a combination solid.

mcqs.q: When computing the surface area of a combination solid, you exclude:
mcqs.explain: Surfaces where the parts meet are hidden, so only exposed surfaces are counted.

mcqs.q: When a solid is melted and recast into another shape, what is conserved?
mcqs.explain: Recasting preserves volume, so equate the two volumes to find unknowns.

u:apt-84-scaling-effects-on-area-and-vol.title: Scaling effects on area and volume
u:apt-84-scaling-effects-on-area-and-vol.summary: Scale length by k: area scales by k^2, volume by k^3.

blocks.text: If every linear dimension is scaled by a factor **k**, then **area scales by k^2** and **volume scales by k^3**. This is why doubling a cube's side multiplies its volume by 8.
If a side increases 20% (k = 1.2), area increases by k^2 - 1 = 0.44 = 44%, and volume by k^3 - 1 = 0.728 = 72.8%. Percentage changes compound via the net-effect formula.

Linear x k → area x k^2 → volume x k^3. This dimensional scaling underlies error-propagation and 'if radius doubles' questions. For small percentage changes, area ~ 2x and volume ~ 3x the linear change.

mcqs.q: If a cube's side is doubled, its volume becomes:
mcqs.explain: Volume scales as k^3 = 2^3 = 8 times.

mcqs.q: Scaling all linear dimensions by 3 multiplies the area by:
mcqs.explain: Area scales as k^2 = 3^2 = 9.

mcqs.q: A radius increased by 10% increases the sphere's volume by about:
mcqs.explain: Volume scales as k^3 = 1.1^3 = 1.331, a 33.1% increase.

u:apt-85-fundamental-counting-principle.title: Fundamental counting principle
u:apt-85-fundamental-counting-principle.summary: Multiply the number of choices at each independent step.

blocks.text: The **fundamental counting principle**: if one task can be done in m ways and another (independent) task in n ways, both together can be done in **m x n** ways. Multiply choices across independent stages.
3 shirts and 4 trousers give 3 x 4 = 12 outfits. A 4-digit PIN (digits 0-9, repetition allowed) = 10^4 = 10000. 'AND' (do both) multiplies; 'OR' (do either) adds.
Multiply for sequential/independent choices ('and'); add for mutually exclusive alternatives ('or'). This principle underlies all permutation and combination counting.

mcqs.q: A menu has 4 starters and 5 mains. The number of starter-main combos is:
mcqs.explain: By the counting principle, 4 x 5 = 20.

mcqs.q: The number of 3-letter codes from 26 letters (repetition allowed) is:
mcqs.explain: Each position has 26 choices independently: 26 x 26 x 26 = 26^3.

mcqs.q: The counting principle says independent stages' choices are:
mcqs.explain: Independent 'and' stages multiply; mutually exclusive 'or' options add.

u:apt-86-permutations-with-repetition.title: Permutations with repetition
u:apt-86-permutations-with-repetition.summary: Order matters; divide by factorials of repeated items when arranging identical objects.

blocks.text: **Permutations** count ORDERED arrangements. nPr = n!/(n-r)!. **Arranging n objects where some are identical**: n! / (p! q! ...) where p, q are counts of each repeated item.
Arrangements of the letters in 'LEVEL' (5 letters: L,E,V,E,L → L twice, E twice) = 5!/(2! 2!) = 120/4 = 30. With repetition allowed in selection (like PIN codes), it's n^r.

Order matters → permutation. For arrangements of items with identical copies, divide n! by the factorial of each repeat count. Distinguish 'repetition allowed' (n^r) from 'identical items' (divide by factorials).

mcqs.q: The number of arrangements of the letters of 'BOOK' is:
mcqs.explain: 4 letters with O repeated twice: 4!/2! = 24/2 = 12.

mcqs.q: nPr (permutations of n taken r) equals:
mcqs.explain: Permutations: nPr = n!/(n-r)! (order matters).

mcqs.q: Arranging n objects where p are identical uses:
mcqs.explain: Divide n! by p! to remove indistinguishable rearrangements of the identical items.

u:apt-87-circular-permutations.title: Circular permutations
u:apt-87-circular-permutations.summary: Arranging n distinct items in a circle gives (n-1)! arrangements.

blocks.text: In a **circular** arrangement, rotations are considered the same, so n distinct objects can be arranged in **(n-1)!** ways (fix one object, arrange the rest). If reflections (clockwise = anticlockwise, e.g. a necklace) are also the same, divide by 2: **(n-1)!/2**.
5 people around a round table: (5-1)! = 24 ways. A necklace of 6 distinct beads: (6-1)!/2 = 60 (flipping it over is not new).
Circular arrangements = (n-1)! because there's no fixed starting position (rotations coincide). Halve it for necklaces/garlands where flipping over is equivalent.

mcqs.q: The number of ways to seat 6 people around a round table is:
Circular permutations of n objects number:
mcqs.explain: Fixing one position to account for rotations gives (n-1)!.

mcqs.q: For a necklace (flips are identical) of n distinct beads, arrangements number:
mcqs.explain: Divide by 2 because a clockwise and its mirror (anticlockwise) reading are the same.

u:apt-88-combinations.title: Combinations
u:apt-88-combinations.summary: Order does not matter; nCr = n!/(r!(n-r)!) counts selections.

blocks.text: **Combinations** count SELECTIONS where order does NOT matter: **nCr = n! / (r!(n-r)!)**. Key identities: nCr = nC(n-r), and nC0 = nCn = 1.
Choosing 3 players from 10: 10C3 = 120. Choosing a committee, a team, a subset → combination (order irrelevant). Arranging them in seats → then multiply by a permutation.
Selection (who/which) = combination; arrangement (in what order) = permutation. nCr = nPr / r!. Use nCr = nC(n-r) to simplify (e.g. 20C18 = 20C2 = 190).

mcqs.q: The number of ways to choose 2 items from 5 is:
mcqs.explain: 5C2 = 10 (order doesn't matter).

mcqs.q: nCr equals:
mcqs.explain: Combinations divide the permutation count by r! since order is irrelevant.

mcqs.q: Which uses combinations rather than permutations?
mcqs.explain: Selecting a committee ignores order — a combination; arranging/ordering uses permutations.

u:apt-89-grouping-and-distribution.title: Grouping and distribution
