u:apt-89-grouping-and-distribution.summary: Divide items into groups by choosing members; identical-group cases need division by k!.

blocks.text: Dividing n items into groups uses combinations. Splitting into groups of sizes r1, r2, ... = **n! / (r1! r2! ...)**. If the groups are the SAME size and unlabelled (indistinguishable), also **divide by k!** (k = number of equal groups).

Divide 12 people into two groups of 6 (unlabelled): 12!/(6!6!) / 2! . Distribute distinct objects into distinct boxes (each can hold any number) = (boxes)^(objects). 'Distinct labelled groups' → no extra division.
Labelled/distinct groups: n!/(r1!r2!...). Unlabelled equal groups: additionally divide by (number of equal groups)! to remove group-order duplication. This distinction is the common trap.

mcqs.q: The number of ways to divide 8 people into two labelled groups of 4 is:
mcqs.explain: 8!/(4!4!) = 70 for distinct/labelled groups.

mcqs.q: For dividing into equal UNLABELLED groups, you additionally divide by:
options: The factorial of the number of equal groups
mcqs.explain: Unlabelled equal groups are interchangeable, so divide by k! to avoid overcounting.

mcqs.q: Distributing r distinct objects into n distinct boxes (any number each) gives:
mcqs.explain: Each of the r objects independently chooses one of n boxes: n^r.

u:apt-90-selection-with-restrictions.title: Selection with restrictions
u:apt-90-selection-with-restrictions.summary: Handle 'must include/exclude' by fixing forced items and 'at least' by complement.

blocks.text: Restricted selection techniques:

items: **Must include** a specific item: fix it, then choose the rest from the remainder.
**Must exclude**: remove it from the pool, then choose.
**At least / at most**: use the **complement** (total minus the unwanted cases) when direct casework is long.
**Together / not together** (arrangements): treat 'together' items as one block; 'not together' = total minus together.

blocks.text: Choose 4 from 10 including a particular person: fix them, choose 3 from remaining 9 = 9C3 = 84. 'At least one girl' = total selections - selections with no girls.
Fix forced inclusions/exclusions first, then count the rest. For 'at least' conditions, the complement (1 - none) is usually faster than summing cases.

mcqs.q: From 8 people, choosing a team of 3 that MUST include a specific person means choosing:
mcqs.explain: Fix the required person, then choose 2 more from the other 7 = 7C2.

mcqs.q: 'At least one' problems are often easiest via:
mcqs.explain: Counting the complement (no successes) and subtracting from the total avoids long casework.

mcqs.q: To count arrangements where two people sit together, you:
options: Treat the pair as a single block, then multiply by 2! for their internal order
mcqs.explain: Glue the pair into one unit (then 2! for their order within the block).

u:apt-91-basic-probability.title: Basic probability
u:apt-91-basic-probability.summary: Probability = favourable outcomes / total outcomes, between 0 and 1.

blocks.text: **Probability of an event = (favourable outcomes) / (total equally-likely outcomes).** It ranges from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). P(not A) = 1 - P(A).
A fair die: P(even) = 3/6 = 1/2. A standard deck (52 cards): P(king) = 4/52 = 1/13. Count favourable and total outcomes carefully — often using combinations.
Set up the sample space (all outcomes) and count favourable ones. The complement rule P(not A) = 1 - P(A) simplifies 'at least' problems. Probabilities always lie in [0,1].

mcqs.q: The probability of rolling a number greater than 4 on a fair die is:
mcqs.explain: Favourable = {5,6} = 2 outcomes out of 6 = 1/3.

mcqs.q: P(not A) equals:
mcqs.explain: The complement of an event has probability 1 minus the event's probability.

mcqs.q: Probability values always lie between:
mcqs.explain: Probability ranges from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain).

u:apt-92-independent-and-dependent-event.title: Independent and dependent events
u:apt-92-independent-and-dependent-event.summary: Independent: multiply probabilities. Dependent: adjust for the changed sample space.

blocks.text: **Independent** events (one doesn't affect the other): P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B). **Dependent** events (the first changes the second's odds, e.g. drawing without replacement): use the updated probability for the second.
Two coin flips (independent): P(both heads) = 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4. Drawing 2 aces without replacement (dependent): 4/52 x 3/51. 'With replacement' → independent; 'without replacement' → dependent.
For 'and' of independent events, multiply. For dependent events, multiply but reduce the counts after each draw. The key cue: replacement (independent) vs no replacement (dependent).

mcqs.q: For two independent events, P(A and B) is:
mcqs.explain: Independent 'and' multiplies the probabilities.

mcqs.q: Drawing two cards WITHOUT replacement makes the events:
mcqs.explain: The first draw changes the deck, so the second's probability depends on it.

mcqs.q: P(two heads in two fair coin flips) is:
mcqs.explain: Independent: 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4.

u:apt-93-conditional-probability.title: Conditional probability
u:apt-93-conditional-probability.summary: P(A given B) = P(A and B) / P(B) - restrict the sample space to B.

blocks.text: **Conditional probability** P(A|B) = **P(A and B) / P(B)** — the probability of A given that B has occurred. It restricts the sample space to outcomes where B is true.
P(a die shows 4 | it shows an even number) = P(4 and even)/P(even) = (1/6)/(1/2) = 1/3. Given B, only B's outcomes are possible, so recompute within that reduced space.
Conditioning shrinks the sample space to B. From P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B) comes the multiplication rule P(A and B) = P(B) x P(A|B), and Bayes' theorem for reversing conditionals.

mcqs.q: P(A given B) is defined as:
mcqs.explain: Conditional probability divides the joint probability by P(B).

mcqs.q: Given a die shows an even number, the probability it is 2 is:
mcqs.explain: Sample space reduces to {2,4,6}; P(2) = 1/3.

mcqs.q: Conditioning on event B:
options: Restricts the sample space to outcomes where B occurs
mcqs.explain: You only consider outcomes consistent with B, then find A's fraction of them.

u:apt-94-probability-with-cards-dice-bal.title: Probability with cards, dice, balls
u:apt-94-probability-with-cards-dice-bal.summary: Standard setups: 52-card decks, dice sums, and drawing balls from urns.

items: **Deck**: 52 cards, 4 suits x 13; 26 red/26 black; 12 face cards; 4 of each rank.
**Two dice**: 36 outcomes; sums range 2-12 (7 is most likely, 6 ways).
**Balls/urns**: use combinations - P = (favourable combinations)/(total combinations).

blocks.text: From an urn with 3 red and 2 blue, P(2 red drawn) = 3C2 / 5C2 = 3/10. Two-dice sum of 7: 6 favourable / 36 = 1/6 (the most common sum).
Memorise the deck composition and two-dice sample space (36 outcomes, 7 most likely). For ball problems, use combinations for both favourable and total counts.

mcqs.q: The probability of drawing a red card from a standard 52-card deck is:
mcqs.explain: 26 red cards out of 52 = 1/2.

mcqs.q: The most likely sum when rolling two dice is:
mcqs.explain: Sum 7 occurs in 6 of 36 ways, the highest of any sum.

mcqs.q: From 4 red and 3 green balls, P(drawing 2 red) is:
mcqs.explain: P = favourable 4C2 = 6 over total 7C2 = 21, i.e. 6/21 = 2/7.

u:apt-95-at-least-one-complement-method.title: At least one / complement method
u:apt-95-at-least-one-complement-method.summary: P(at least one) = 1 - P(none) - far easier than summing cases.

blocks.text: For 'at least one' problems, compute the **complement**: **P(at least one) = 1 - P(none).** This avoids adding up 'exactly 1, exactly 2, ...' cases.
P(at least one head in 3 coin flips) = 1 - P(no heads) = 1 - (1/2)^3 = 1 - 1/8 = 7/8. For independent trials, P(none) is the product of each trial's failure probability.
'At least one' → 1 minus 'none'. This is the single most useful probability shortcut: computing the one complement case beats summing many favourable cases.

mcqs.q: P(at least one six in two dice rolls) is:
The complement method computes 'at least one' as:
mcqs.explain: Subtracting the single 'none' case from 1 is far faster than casework.

mcqs.q: For 4 independent trials each failing with probability 0.5, P(at least one success) is:

u:apt-96-single-table.title: Single table
u:apt-96-single-table.summary: Read rows and columns carefully; most questions are totals, differences, and percentages.

blocks.text: A **table DI** presents data in rows and columns. Questions ask for totals, differences, ratios, averages, and percentage comparisons. The skill is careful reading plus fast percentage arithmetic.

items: Read row/column headers precisely; note units and any footnotes.
Common asks: total of a row/column, percentage change between two cells, ratio of two values, which is highest/lowest.
Approximate when options are far apart to save time.

blocks.text: Table DI has no new theory — it's percentages, ratios, and averages applied to grid data. Accuracy in reading the right cell and speed in estimation win marks.

mcqs.q: Most single-table DI questions reduce to:
mcqs.explain: Table interpretation applies basic arithmetic operations to the grid values.

mcqs.q: The most common reading error in table DI is:
options: Misreading the wrong row/column or ignoring units
mcqs.explain: Picking the wrong cell or missing a unit/footnote is the top mistake.

mcqs.q: When answer options are widely spaced, you should:
mcqs.explain: Estimation is safe and fast when precision isn't needed to distinguish options.

u:apt-97-multi-table-comparison.title: Multi-table comparison
u:apt-97-multi-table-comparison.summary: Cross-reference two or more tables; track which table each value comes from.

blocks.text: **Multi-table DI** requires combining data from two or more linked tables (e.g. one gives quantities, another gives prices, or one is per-year and another per-category).
If Table 1 gives units sold and Table 2 gives price per unit, revenue = units x price, pulling one number from each table. Carefully match the same category/year across tables.
The challenge is cross-referencing accurately: identify which table supplies each figure and ensure you match the same category/period. Then it's ordinary arithmetic.

mcqs.q: Multi-table DI primarily tests your ability to:
options: Cross-reference and combine data from multiple tables correctly
mcqs.explain: You must pull matching figures from different tables and combine them.

mcqs.q: To compute revenue when units and price are in separate tables:
options: Multiply units (table 1) by price (table 2) for the matching item
mcqs.explain: Revenue = units x price, taking each factor from its respective table for the same item.

mcqs.q: The key risk in multi-table DI is:
mcqs.explain: Combining figures for different categories or years produces wrong answers.

u:apt-98-missing-value-tables.title: Missing value tables
u:apt-98-missing-value-tables.summary: Use row/column totals and given relationships to fill blanks before answering.

blocks.text: **Missing-value tables** leave some cells blank; you deduce them from **totals**, **given ratios/percentages**, or relationships stated in the question, then answer.
If a row total is given and all but one cell are known, the missing cell = total - sum of the others. If a percentage of the total is given, back-calculate the value.
Fill in the blanks FIRST using totals and stated conditions, then treat it as an ordinary table. Don't attempt questions before completing the necessary cells.

mcqs.q: A row total is 200; three of four cells are 40, 60, and 30. The missing cell is:
Missing values are typically found using:
mcqs.explain: Totals and given relationships let you deduce the blanks.

mcqs.q: The correct order for missing-value DI is to:
options: Fill the needed blanks first, then answer
mcqs.explain: Deduce the missing figures before computing the requested quantities.

u:apt-99-simple-bar.title: Simple bar
u:apt-99-simple-bar.summary: Bar height equals value; compare, sum, and compute percentage changes across bars.

blocks.text: A **bar chart** shows values as bar heights across categories (e.g. sales per year). Read each bar's value from the axis; questions ask comparisons, totals, averages, and percentage change between bars.
Percentage growth from year A to year B = (barB - barA)/barA x 100. The average = sum of bar values / number of bars. Read heights carefully against the gridlines.
Bar height = value. Everything else is the usual percentage/ratio/average arithmetic. Precise reading off the axis is the main skill.

mcqs.q: In a bar chart, a bar's value is given by its:
mcqs.explain: The height of each bar represents its value on the vertical axis.

mcqs.q: Percentage increase from a bar of 200 to a bar of 250 is:
The average of the bars equals:
options: Sum of values / number of bars
mcqs.explain: Average = total of all bar values divided by their count.

u:apt-100-stacked-bar.title: Stacked bar
u:apt-100-stacked-bar.summary: Each bar is split into segments; segment height is that component's value.

blocks.text: A **stacked bar** divides each bar into segments representing sub-categories, stacked on top of each other. The **total bar height** = the category total; each **segment's height** = that component's value.
To read a segment's value, subtract the cumulative height below it from the height at its top. Percentage of a component = segment value / total bar height x 100.
Segment value = (top of segment) - (bottom of segment). The whole bar gives the total; segments give the composition. Watch for reading cumulative heights instead of segment sizes.

mcqs.q: In a stacked bar, the total value of a category is shown by:
options: The full height of the whole bar
mcqs.explain: The complete bar height is the sum (total) of all its segments.

mcqs.q: A single component's value in a stacked bar is:
options: The height of that segment (top minus bottom)
mcqs.explain: Each segment's own height (its span) is that component's value.

mcqs.q: A component's percentage share equals:
mcqs.explain: Share of total = the segment's value divided by the whole bar's total.

u:apt-101-grouped-bar.title: Grouped bar
u:apt-101-grouped-bar.summary: Bars are clustered by category to compare sub-groups side by side.

blocks.text: A **grouped (clustered) bar chart** places multiple bars side by side within each category (e.g. sales of product A vs B vs C for each year), to compare sub-groups directly.
Each bar in a group is read separately (unlike stacked, they don't add up within the group visually). To compare a sub-group across categories, track the same-coloured bar across groups.
Grouped bars sit SIDE BY SIDE (compare within a group); stacked bars sit ON TOP (show composition/total). Read each grouped bar's height independently.

mcqs.q: In a grouped bar chart, bars within a group are:
options: Placed side by side for direct comparison
mcqs.explain: Clustered bars sit side by side to compare sub-groups within each category.

mcqs.q: Grouped bars differ from stacked bars because grouped bars:
options: Add up to a total visually
Are compared side by side (each read separately)
mcqs.explain: Grouped compares sub-groups side by side; stacked composes them into a total.

mcqs.q: To track one product across years in a grouped chart, follow:
options: The same-coloured bar in each group
mcqs.explain: Each sub-group is a consistent colour; follow it across the category groups.

u:apt-102-single-pie.title: Single pie
u:apt-102-single-pie.summary: A pie shows shares of a whole; 360 degrees or 100% represents the total.

blocks.text: A **pie chart** shows each category's share of a whole. The full circle = **360 degrees = 100% = the total**. A category's degree = (its value/total) x 360; its percentage = (value/total) x 100.
A sector of 90 degrees is 90/360 = 25% of the total. If the total is given (say 8000) and a sector is 45 degrees, its value = 45/360 x 8000 = 1000. Convert between degrees, percent, and value freely.
Three interchangeable representations: degrees (out of 360), percent (out of 100), and absolute value (out of the total). 1% = 3.6 degrees. Convert to whichever the question needs.

mcqs.q: A pie sector of 72 degrees represents what percent of the total?
In a pie chart, 1% of the total corresponds to how many degrees?
mcqs.explain: 360/100 = 3.6 degrees per percent.

mcqs.q: If the total is 5000 and a sector is 90 degrees, its value is:

u:apt-103-two-pies-compared.title: Two pies compared
u:apt-103-two-pies-compared.summary: Two pies may have different totals - convert percentages to absolute values before comparing.

blocks.text: When comparing **two pie charts**, note that each may represent a **different total**. A larger percentage in one pie can be a smaller absolute value if that pie's total is smaller.

Pie A (total 2000) shows 30% for X = 600; Pie B (total 5000) shows 20% for X = 1000. Despite the higher percentage in A, B's absolute value is larger. Always convert to actual values before comparing.
Percentages are relative to each pie's own total. To compare quantities across two pies, convert both to absolute values using their respective totals. Comparing raw percentages is the classic trap.

mcqs.q: To compare a category's actual quantity across two pies, you must:
options: Convert each percentage to an absolute value using each pie's total
mcqs.explain: The pies may have different totals, so percentages aren't directly comparable.

mcqs.q: A higher percentage in one pie means a higher absolute value only if:
options: The totals are equal (or the smaller-percent pie's total isn't much larger)
mcqs.explain: With different totals, a smaller percentage of a larger total can exceed a larger percentage of a smaller total.

mcqs.q: Pie A total 1000 with 40% vs Pie B total 3000 with 20% for item X. Larger actual X is in:
mcqs.explain: A: 400; B: 600 — B is larger despite the smaller percentage.

u:apt-104-pie-with-absolute-values.title: Pie with absolute values
u:apt-104-pie-with-absolute-values.summary: When the total is given, convert any sector to its actual value with degree or percent share.

blocks.text: When a pie chart is accompanied by the **total value**, you can convert any sector's degree or percentage into an **absolute value**: sector value = (sector percent) x total, or (sector degrees/360) x total.
Total expenditure 12000; 'Rent' = 25%: rent = 0.25 x 12000 = 3000. Combine sectors by adding their percentages first, then applying to the total (e.g. rent + food = 40% = 4800).
With the total known, everything becomes an absolute value via multiplication. Add sector percentages before multiplying to combine categories efficiently.

mcqs.q: Total budget 20000; a sector is 15%. Its value is:
To combine two sectors' values, you should:
options: Add their percentages, then multiply by the total
mcqs.explain: Sum the percentage shares first, then apply to the total for the combined value.

mcqs.q: Total 9000; a sector of 120 degrees has value:

u:apt-105-bar-line.title: Bar + line
u:apt-105-bar-line.summary: Combo charts overlay a line (often a rate/percentage) on bars (often absolute values).

blocks.text: A **bar + line combo** chart shows two related datasets: usually **bars for absolute values** (e.g. revenue) and a **line for a rate or percentage** (e.g. growth %, margin %). Read each from its own axis (often dual axes).
Check which axis each series uses — combo charts often have two vertical axes with different scales. Compute derived values by combining a bar (absolute) with its line value (rate).
Identify what the bars and the line each represent, and which axis each uses. Mixing up the two scales is the main pitfall. Then apply standard arithmetic.

mcqs.q: In a bar+line combo chart, the line typically represents:
options: A rate or percentage (e.g. growth %), often on a second axis
mcqs.explain: The line usually shows a rate/percentage while bars show absolute values.

mcqs.q: The main pitfall in combo charts is:
mcqs.explain: Dual axes have different scales; misreading which applies causes errors.

mcqs.q: To read a combo chart correctly, first identify:
options: What each series represents and which axis it uses
mcqs.explain: Knowing each series' meaning and axis is essential before computing.

u:apt-106-pie-table.title: Pie + table
u:apt-106-pie-table.summary: Combine a pie's shares with a table's absolute values (or vice versa) to answer.

blocks.text: A **pie + table** combo gives a pie for proportional breakdown and a table for related absolute figures (or a further sub-breakdown). You cross-reference the two: apply the pie's percentage to a table total, or split a table value by the pie.
Pie shows department-wise budget share; a table shows the total budget per year. Department X's budget in year Y = (X's pie %) x (year Y total from table).
Use the pie for proportions and the table for actual totals, multiplying to get absolute values. The skill is correctly matching which pie share applies to which table figure.

mcqs.q: In a pie+table combo, you typically compute a value by:
options: Applying the pie's percentage share to a total from the table
mcqs.explain: The pie gives the proportion; the table gives the total to which it's applied.

mcqs.q: The pie chart in such a combo provides:
mcqs.explain: Pies show relative shares; the table usually supplies the absolute totals.

mcqs.q: The key skill in pie+table DI is:
options: Matching the correct pie share to the correct table total
mcqs.explain: Correctly cross-referencing the two sources is essential for the right value.

u:apt-107-caselet-di.title: Caselet DI
u:apt-107-caselet-di.summary: Data given as a paragraph - extract the numbers into a table before solving.

blocks.text: A **caselet** presents DI data as a **paragraph of text** rather than a chart or table. The first step is to **extract the numbers and relationships into your own table/diagram**, then solve as usual.
Read carefully, note each given value and relationship (ratios, totals, differences), and build a small table. Caselets often hide the data among words, so structured extraction prevents mistakes.
Convert the prose into a table FIRST. Caselet DI tests reading comprehension plus arithmetic — once the data is organised, it's an ordinary DI problem.

mcqs.q: The first step in solving a caselet DI is to:
options: Extract the numbers/relationships from the text into a table
mcqs.explain: Organising the prose data into a structured form makes it solvable like any DI.

mcqs.q: Caselet DI mainly adds which challenge over a table?
options: Reading and extracting data from prose
mcqs.explain: The data is embedded in text, testing careful reading before the arithmetic.

mcqs.q: After extracting the data, a caselet becomes:
mcqs.explain: Once organised, it's solved with the same percentage/ratio methods as any DI.

u:apt-108-arithmetic-and-geometric-serie.title: Arithmetic and geometric series
u:apt-108-arithmetic-and-geometric-serie.summary: AP adds a constant difference; GP multiplies by a constant ratio.

blocks.text: **Arithmetic Progression (AP)**: each term adds a constant **d** (common difference). nth term = a + (n-1)d; sum = n/2 [2a + (n-1)d]. **Geometric Progression (GP)**: each term multiplies by a constant **r**. nth term = a*r^(n-1); sum = a(r^n - 1)/(r-1).
AP 3, 7, 11, 15... (d=4). GP 2, 6, 18, 54... (r=3). To identify a number series: check if differences are constant (AP) or ratios are constant (GP).
AP = constant DIFFERENCE (add d); GP = constant RATIO (multiply by r). Checking differences vs ratios is the first move in any 'find the next term' series problem.

mcqs.q: The next term in the series 5, 10, 20, 40, ... is:
mcqs.explain: It's a GP with ratio 2: 40 x 2 = 80.

mcqs.q: In an arithmetic progression, consecutive terms have a constant:
mcqs.explain: AP adds a fixed common difference d each step.

mcqs.q: The nth term of an AP with first term a and difference d is:
mcqs.explain: AP nth term = a + (n-1)d.

u:apt-109-mixed-operation-series.title: Mixed operation series
u:apt-109-mixed-operation-series.summary: Terms change by alternating or escalating operations - find the pattern in the changes.

blocks.text: In **mixed-operation series**, the rule combines operations (e.g. x2 then +1, or +2, +4, +8, or alternate + and x). Look at the pattern in how each term is derived from the previous.
Series 2, 5, 11, 23, 47: each term is x2 + 1 (2x2+1=5, 5x2+1=11...). Or 1, 2, 6, 24, 120: multiply by 1, 2, 3, 4 (factorials). Check both the differences AND the ratios, and whether they escalate.
Examine the operation between terms: is it a constant op, an alternating op, or an escalating one (differences that themselves form a pattern)? Test x2+1, squares, cubes, and factorial patterns.

mcqs.q: Find the next term: 3, 7, 15, 31, ...
For mixed-operation series, you should check:
options: Both differences and ratios, and whether they escalate
mcqs.explain: The rule may combine or escalate operations, so test multiple relationships.

mcqs.q: The series 1, 2, 6, 24, 120 follows the rule:
mcqs.explain: Each term multiplies the previous by an increasing integer (n!).

u:apt-110-wrong-term-identification.title: Wrong term identification
u:apt-110-wrong-term-identification.summary: Establish the intended pattern, then find the single term that breaks it.

blocks.text: In **'find the wrong term'** questions, most terms follow a pattern but one is off. Identify the intended rule from the majority of terms, then locate the term that doesn't fit and note what it should be.
Series 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, 44 (should be differences 4,6,8,10,12 giving ...42, so 44 is wrong). Establish the pattern from the correct terms first, then check each candidate.
Deduce the rule from the terms that agree, then the odd one out is the term violating it. Verify by computing what the value should have been.

mcqs.q: The approach to a 'find the wrong term' series is to:
options: Establish the pattern from most terms, then find the one that breaks it
mcqs.explain: The intended rule emerges from the majority; the outlier is the wrong term.

mcqs.q: In 3, 6, 12, 24, 50, 96 (doubling), the wrong term is:
mcqs.explain: Doubling gives 48, not 50, so 50 is the wrong term.

mcqs.q: After finding the wrong term, you should:
options: Note the correct value it should have been
mcqs.explain: Confirming the correct value verifies you identified the right pattern.

u:apt-111-letter-series.title: Letter series
u:apt-111-letter-series.summary: Map letters to positions (A=1...Z=26) and find the jump pattern.

blocks.text: In a **letter series**, convert letters to positions (A=1, B=2, ... Z=26) and find the pattern in the position jumps (like a number series). Watch for wrap-around after Z back to A.
Series A, C, E, G, ... skips one letter each time (+2): next is I. B, D, G, K, ... jumps +2, +3, +4: next is P (K+5). Assign numbers to see the jumps clearly.
Number the alphabet, then the letter series becomes a number series. Common patterns: fixed skip, increasing skip, or a two-interleaved sequence. Remember Z (26) wraps to A (1).

mcqs.q: Find the next letter: A, C, E, G, ...
mcqs.explain: Each step +2 positions: G(7) + 2 = I(9).

mcqs.q: The technique for letter series is to:
options: Convert letters to positions (A=1...) and analyse the jumps
mcqs.explain: Numbering the alphabet turns it into a familiar number-pattern problem.

mcqs.q: In the alphabet numbering, after Z (26) the next wraps to:
mcqs.explain: Series often wrap cyclically from Z back to A.

u:apt-112-alphanumeric-series.title: Alphanumeric series
u:apt-112-alphanumeric-series.summary: Mixed letters, numbers, and symbols - answer by counting positions per the condition.

blocks.text: An **alphanumeric series** mixes letters, digits, and symbols in a sequence. Questions ask things like 'how many digits are immediately followed by a letter?' or 'which element is 3rd to the left of the 5th number?'. The skill is careful positional counting against the stated condition.
Read the condition precisely ('immediately preceded by a symbol AND followed by a number') and scan the string element by element, marking matches. Track direction (left/right) carefully.
These test attention to detail: parse the exact condition, then scan systematically. Miscounting position or misreading 'preceded' vs 'followed' is the main error.

mcqs.q: Alphanumeric series questions mainly test:
options: Careful positional counting against a stated condition
mcqs.explain: You scan a mixed string and count elements matching precise conditions.

mcqs.q: A common trap in these questions is:
options: Confusing 'preceded by' with 'followed by' or miscounting positions
mcqs.explain: Direction and exact position wording are easy to misread.

mcqs.q: The best method is to:
options: Scan the string systematically, marking matches to the exact condition
mcqs.explain: Systematic scanning against the precise condition avoids counting errors.

u:apt-113-continuous-pattern.title: Continuous pattern
u:apt-113-continuous-pattern.summary: Fill blanks in a repeating letter/symbol pattern by identifying the repeating unit.

blocks.text: A **continuous pattern** series has a repeating block with some positions blank; you fill the blanks so the pattern continues consistently. Identify the **repeating unit** (cycle), then place letters accordingly.
For a pattern like a_bb_aa_bba_ , find the repeating group (e.g. 'aabb') and fill blanks to match. Divide the string into equal blocks to reveal the cycle.
Find the length of the repeating cycle, then each blank is determined by its position within the cycle. Splitting the string into equal segments makes the pattern visible.

mcqs.q: To solve continuous pattern (fill-the-blank) questions, first identify the:
mcqs.explain: The repeating block determines what each blank must be.

mcqs.q: A useful technique is to:
options: Split the string into equal blocks to reveal the cycle
mcqs.explain: Dividing into equal segments exposes the repeating pattern.

mcqs.q: Each blank in a continuous pattern is fixed by its:
mcqs.explain: Its place in the cycle determines the required letter/symbol.

u:apt-114-letter-coding.title: Letter coding
u:apt-114-letter-coding.summary: Decode by finding the positional shift between plaintext and code letters.

blocks.text: In **letter coding**, a word is encoded by shifting each letter a fixed number of positions (like a Caesar cipher) or by another letter-position rule. Find the **shift** by comparing a known letter to its code.
If CAT is coded as ECV, each letter moved +2 (C->E, A->C, T->V). Apply the same +2 to decode/encode other words. Some codes reverse (A=Z, B=Y...) or use the opposite position (27 - n).
Compare corresponding letters to find the rule (fixed forward/backward shift, reversal, or opposite-position). Then apply it consistently. Number the alphabet to see the shift clearly.

mcqs.q: If DOG is coded as FQI, the shift applied is:
mcqs.explain: D->F, O->Q, G->I is each +2 positions.

mcqs.q: The first step in letter coding is to:
options: Compare a plaintext letter with its code to find the shift/rule
mcqs.explain: Matching known letters to their codes reveals the encoding rule.

mcqs.q: 'Opposite letter' coding maps A to:
mcqs.explain: Opposite-position coding pairs A<->Z, B<->Y, etc. (position 27 - n).

u:apt-115-number-coding.title: Number coding
u:apt-115-number-coding.summary: Letters/words map to numbers by position, sum, or a fixed operation - find the rule.

blocks.text: In **number coding**, words or letters are assigned numbers by a rule: letter positions (A=1...), a sum/product of positions, or an arithmetic operation on the positions. Deduce the rule from given examples.
If 'CAB' is coded 312, the numbers are the reversed positions (C=3, A=1, B=2). If a word maps to a single number, check the sum of letter positions or their product. Test simple operations first.
Try letter-position mappings and simple aggregations (sum, product) of positions. Once the rule fits the given examples, apply it to the target. Systematic testing beats guessing.

mcqs.q: If A=1, B=2..., the code for 'BAD' as position-sum is:
To crack number coding, you should:
options: Test position mappings and simple operations (sum/product) against the examples
mcqs.explain: Fitting a simple rule to the given examples reveals the encoding.

mcqs.q: If a whole word maps to one number, a good first check is:
options: The sum (or product) of letter positions
mcqs.explain: Aggregating letter positions (sum/product) is a common single-number coding rule.

u:apt-116-substitution-coding.title: Substitution coding
u:apt-116-substitution-coding.summary: Words are replaced by other words; map meanings by cross-referencing sentences.

blocks.text: In **substitution coding**, real words are replaced by code words (e.g. 'sky' means 'blue'). Given several coded sentences, deduce each code word's meaning by finding **common words across sentences** and matching them to common code words.
If two sentences share a real word AND share a code word, that code word likely means that real word. Cross-reference multiple statements to pin down each mapping, then translate the target.
The method is elimination by overlap: shared meanings across sentences correspond to shared code words. Build the dictionary word by word, then decode the question.

mcqs.q: In substitution coding, code word meanings are found by:
options: Cross-referencing common words/code words across multiple sentences
mcqs.explain: Overlapping words and codes across statements reveal each mapping.

mcqs.q: If two coded sentences share one real word and one code word, that code word likely means:
mcqs.explain: The common code corresponds to the common meaning across the sentences.

mcqs.q: The technique is essentially:
options: Elimination by overlap to build a dictionary
mcqs.explain: You deduce mappings by matching overlaps, forming a code-to-meaning dictionary.

u:apt-117-conditional-coding.title: Conditional coding
u:apt-117-conditional-coding.summary: Apply given rules in order; watch for exception conditions that override the defaults.

blocks.text: In **conditional coding**, a set of rules assigns symbols/codes to elements, with **exception conditions** that override the default in certain cases (e.g. 'if the first element is a vowel and the last is a consonant, swap their codes').

Apply the default coding first, then check each stated condition in order and apply any that fits (only one usually applies). Read exceptions precisely — they often hinge on the first/last element's type.
Default rule first, then exception conditions. Check conditions carefully and in the given priority; typically at most one exception applies. Missing an exception is the main error.

mcqs.q: In conditional coding, exception conditions:
options: Override the default coding in specific cases
mcqs.explain: Exceptions replace the default only when their stated condition is met.

mcqs.q: The correct order is to:
options: Apply the default, then check and apply any matching exception
mcqs.explain: Establish the default codes, then override where a condition fits.

mcqs.q: The main error in conditional coding is:
mcqs.explain: Missing a triggered exception yields the wrong code; read conditions precisely.

u:apt-118-angle-between-hands.title: Angle between hands
u:apt-118-angle-between-hands.summary: Angle = |30H - 5.5M| degrees; take the smaller of it and 360 minus it.

blocks.text: The angle between the hour and minute hands at H:M is **|30H - 5.5M|** degrees. The minute hand moves 6 deg/min; the hour hand 0.5 deg/min (so it drifts past the hour mark).
At 4:20: |30x4 - 5.5x20| = |120 - 110| = 10 degrees. The hands coincide (0 degrees) 11 times in 12 hours, and are opposite (180) 11 times too. If the formula exceeds 180, subtract from 360.
Memorise |30H - 5.5M|. The common mistake is forgetting the hour hand moves as minutes pass (the 5.5, not 6). The hands overlap every 65 5/11 minutes.

mcqs.q: The angle between the hands at 6:00 is:
mcqs.explain: |30x6 - 5.5x0| = 180 degrees (hands opposite).

mcqs.q: The angle-between-hands formula is:
mcqs.explain: Hour hand 30H + 0.5M, minute hand 6M; difference is |30H - 5.5M|.

mcqs.q: In 12 hours, the hands overlap (0 degrees):
mcqs.explain: The hands coincide 11 times every 12 hours.

u:apt-119-incorrect-clocks.title: Incorrect clocks
u:apt-119-incorrect-clocks.summary: A clock gaining/losing time drifts by a fixed amount per hour - scale up over the period.

blocks.text: A **faulty clock** gains or loses a fixed amount of time per period. To find the total error, scale the per-hour (or per-day) drift over the elapsed time, then adjust the shown time.

A clock gaining 2 minutes per hour will be 48 minutes fast after 24 hours. If it was correct at noon, after 24 hours it shows 12:48. Set up a proportion: error is directly proportional to elapsed time.

Error is proportional to elapsed time. Also, a clock's hands coincide every 65 5/11 minutes of TRUE time; if a clock shows overlaps at a different interval, it's running fast or slow — a classic trick.

mcqs.q: A clock gains 3 minutes per hour. After 8 hours it is:
mcqs.explain: 3 x 8 = 24 minutes gained (fast).

mcqs.q: The error of a faulty clock is ______ to the elapsed time.
mcqs.explain: A fixed drift per hour accumulates linearly with time.

mcqs.q: A correct clock's hands coincide every:
mcqs.explain: True overlaps occur every 65 5/11 minutes; a different interval means the clock is inaccurate.

u:apt-120-odd-days-and-day-of-week.title: Odd days and day of week
u:apt-120-odd-days-and-day-of-week.summary: Count 'odd days' (days beyond complete weeks) to find the day of the week.

blocks.text: **Odd days** = days left over after removing complete weeks (remainder when total days are divided by 7). They shift the day of the week. This is how to find what day a date falls on.

items: Ordinary year = 365 days = 52 weeks + **1 odd day**. Leap year = **2 odd days**.
100 years = 5 odd days; 200 = 3; 300 = 1; 400 = 0 odd days.
Add up odd days from a reference date; the total mod 7 gives the day shift.

blocks.text: Each ordinary year advances the calendar by 1 weekday (e.g. if Jan 1 is Monday this year, next year it's Tuesday), and a leap year advances by 2. Count odd days carefully across the period.
Odd days = total days mod 7. Ordinary year = 1, leap = 2. Summing odd days from a known day and taking mod 7 pinpoints any date's weekday.

mcqs.q: An ordinary (non-leap) year has how many odd days?
mcqs.explain: 365 = 52 weeks + 1 day, so 1 odd day.

mcqs.q: A leap year has how many odd days?
mcqs.explain: 366 = 52 weeks + 2 days, so 2 odd days.

mcqs.q: Odd days are found by taking the total number of days:
mcqs.explain: The remainder after removing complete weeks gives the odd days.

u:apt-121-leap-year-logic.title: Leap year logic
u:apt-121-leap-year-logic.summary: Divisible by 4, except centuries which must be divisible by 400.

blocks.text: A year is a **leap year** if it is **divisible by 4**, EXCEPT century years (divisible by 100), which are leap only if **divisible by 400**.
2024 (div by 4) = leap. 1900 (div by 100 but not 400) = NOT leap. 2000 (div by 400) = leap. This exception is why 100 years have 24 leap years, not 25.
Rule: divisible by 4 → leap, unless divisible by 100 → not leap, unless divisible by 400 → leap. The century exception (100/400) is the tested subtlety and affects odd-day counts.

mcqs.q: Which year is a leap year?
mcqs.explain: 2000 is divisible by 400, so it's a leap year; 1900 and 2100 are centuries not divisible by 400.

mcqs.q: A century year is a leap year only if divisible by:
mcqs.explain: Century years need divisibility by 400 to be leap years.

mcqs.q: Is 1600 a leap year?
mcqs.explain: 1600 is divisible by 400, so it is a leap year.

u:apt-122-direct-relation-puzzles.title: Direct relation puzzles
u:apt-122-direct-relation-puzzles.summary: Draw a family tree, using symbols for gender and generation, to trace relationships.

blocks.text: **Blood relation** questions describe how people are related; the reliable method is to **draw a family tree**. Use symbols: + for male, - for female, a horizontal line for spouse/siblings, a vertical line for parent-child (generations).

Read one clue at a time and place each person on the diagram. 'A is B's father's sister' → go up from B to father, then sideways to his sister = A (aunt). Keep generations on the same horizontal level.
Always diagram it — don't hold relations in your head. Same generation on the same level; parents above, children below. This prevents the confusion these puzzles are designed to cause.

mcqs.q: The most reliable method for blood-relation puzzles is to:
mcqs.explain: A diagram tracks generations and gender, preventing confusion.

mcqs.q: In a family tree, people of the same generation are placed:
mcqs.explain: Same generation sits on one level; parent-child links are vertical.

mcqs.q: 'My father's sister' is your:
mcqs.explain: The father's sister is your (paternal) aunt.

u:apt-123-coded-relations.title: Coded relations
u:apt-123-coded-relations.summary: Symbols encode relationships; decode the expression step by step, respecting order.

blocks.text: In **coded blood relations**, symbols represent relationships (e.g. A + B means A is the father of B; A - B means A is the wife of B). Decode expressions **step by step in the given order**, building the relationship chain.
For 'A + B - C', apply A+B first (A is father of B), then B-C (B is wife of C), giving A is C's father-in-law (via his daughter B). Work left to right, drawing as you go.
Translate each symbol using the given legend, process left to right, and diagram the chain. The final relationship is read from the completed tree, respecting gender from the symbols.

mcqs.q: To solve coded relation expressions, you should:
options: Decode each symbol per the legend, left to right, and diagram it
mcqs.explain: Applying the defined symbol meanings in order builds the correct relationship.

mcqs.q: Coded relation expressions are processed:
options: Left to right (in the given order)
mcqs.explain: Order matters; evaluate the chain in the sequence given.

mcqs.q: The final relationship is determined by:
options: The completed relationship chain (with gender from symbols)
mcqs.explain: Read the answer from the full diagram, using gender indicated by the symbols.

u:apt-124-family-tree-with-gender-clues.title: Family tree with gender clues
u:apt-124-family-tree-with-gender-clues.summary: Track gender carefully; ambiguous relations (like 'cousin') can hide the intended answer.

blocks.text: Complex family-tree puzzles hinge on **correctly assigning gender** and reading relationship words precisely. Some terms (cousin, in-law, sibling) don't specify gender, and puzzles exploit this.
Mark each person's gender as soon as a clue reveals it (e.g. 'his son', 'her mother'). Don't assume gender from names or roles. Watch for terms like 'spouse' or 'child' that are gender-neutral.
Gender is the most common source of errors. Annotate the tree with M/F as clues confirm them, and never infer gender from a name. Only conclude what the clues actually establish.

mcqs.q: The most common error in family-tree puzzles is:
mcqs.explain: Gender mistakes (or assuming gender from names) lead to wrong relationships.

mcqs.q: You should determine a person's gender from:
mcqs.explain: Only stated clues reliably fix gender; names and roles can mislead.

mcqs.q: Which relationship term is gender-neutral?
mcqs.explain: 'Cousin' (like spouse, child, sibling) doesn't specify gender.

u:apt-125-basic-direction-tracing.title: Basic direction tracing
u:apt-125-basic-direction-tracing.summary: Draw the path on a grid; track net displacement using the compass.

blocks.text: **Direction sense** questions describe a path (walk N, turn right, etc.); trace it on paper using a compass (N up, E right, S down, W left). Track the net displacement to answer 'how far and in which direction from the start?'
A right turn rotates you 90 degrees clockwise (N->E->S->W->N); a left turn 90 degrees anticlockwise. Net East-West and North-South displacements combine via Pythagoras for straight-line distance.
Always sketch it with the compass fixed. Sum movements along each axis (net N-S and net E-W); the final direction and distance follow from those two components.

mcqs.q: Facing North, a right turn makes you face:
mcqs.explain: A right (clockwise) turn from North faces East.

mcqs.q: The straight-line distance from start given net N-S and E-W displacements is found using:
mcqs.explain: The two perpendicular components combine as sqrt(NS^2 + EW^2).

mcqs.q: The reliable method for direction problems is to:
options: Sketch the path with a fixed compass
mcqs.explain: Drawing the path keeps turns and net displacement accurate.

u:apt-126-shadow-based-direction.title: Shadow-based direction
u:apt-126-shadow-based-direction.summary: Shadows fall opposite the sun: west in the morning, east in the evening.

blocks.text: **Shadow direction** problems use the sun's position. In the **morning** the sun is in the East, so shadows fall toward the **West**. In the **evening** the sun is in the West, so shadows fall toward the **East**. At noon, shadows are minimal/absent.
If a person's shadow falls to their right in the morning (sun in East, shadow to West), they must be facing North. Use the sun's side to fix the shadow's direction, then deduce the facing.
Shadow is always OPPOSITE the sun. Morning sun (East) → shadow West; evening sun (West) → shadow East. From the shadow's relative position (left/right/front), work out which way the person faces.

mcqs.q: In the morning, shadows fall toward the:
mcqs.explain: The morning sun is in the East, so shadows point West (opposite the sun).

mcqs.q: In the evening, shadows fall toward the:
mcqs.explain: The evening sun is in the West, so shadows point East.

mcqs.q: A shadow always points:
mcqs.explain: Shadows fall on the side away from the light source (the sun).

u:apt-127-distance-calculation.title: Distance calculation
u:apt-127-distance-calculation.summary: Combine net displacements with Pythagoras for straight-line distance.

blocks.text: After tracing a path, find the **straight-line (shortest) distance** from start to end using the net displacements. If net East-West = x and net North-South = y, distance = **sqrt(x^2 + y^2)**.
Walk 3 km East, 4 km North: distance from start = sqrt(3^2 + 4^2) = 5 km (a 3-4-5 triangle). Cancel opposite movements first (e.g. 5 km East then 2 km West = net 3 km East).
Net the movements along each axis (opposite directions cancel), then apply Pythagoras. Knowing common triples (3-4-5, 5-12-13) makes this instant.

mcqs.q: Net displacements of 6 km East and 8 km North give a straight-line distance of:
Before applying Pythagoras, you should:
options: Net opposite-direction movements along each axis
mcqs.explain: Cancel opposite moves to get the net displacement on each axis first.

mcqs.q: Walking 5 km North then 5 km South leaves a net north-south displacement of:
mcqs.explain: Equal opposite moves cancel, giving zero net displacement on that axis.

u:apt-128-two-statement-syllogism.title: Two-statement syllogism
u:apt-128-two-statement-syllogism.summary: Use Venn diagrams; a conclusion is valid only if it MUST follow from the statements.

blocks.text: A **syllogism** gives statements ('All A are B', 'Some B are C') and asks which conclusions **definitely follow**. The reliable method is **Venn diagrams**: a conclusion is valid only if it holds in EVERY possible diagram consistent with the statements.

items: 'All A are B' → circle A inside B. 'No A are B' → separate circles. 'Some A are B' → overlapping.
A conclusion is valid only if it's true in all valid arrangements (not just one).
Assume ONLY what's stated — don't add outside knowledge.

blocks.text: Validity means 'necessarily true in every case'. If you can draw even one consistent diagram where the conclusion fails, it does NOT follow. Diagram, don't reason verbally.

mcqs.q: A syllogism conclusion is valid only if it:
options: Must be true in every possible diagram
mcqs.explain: Validity requires the conclusion to hold in all arrangements consistent with the premises.

mcqs.q: 'All cats are animals' is drawn as:
options: Cats circle inside the Animals circle
mcqs.explain: 'All A are B' places A entirely within B.

mcqs.q: If a conclusion fails in even one valid diagram, it:
mcqs.explain: A single counter-arrangement means the conclusion is not necessarily true.

u:apt-129-three-statement.title: Three-statement
u:apt-129-three-statement.summary: More premises mean more relationships - diagram all three and check conclusions against every case.

blocks.text: **Three-statement syllogisms** add a premise, so the Venn diagram has more circles and relationships. The method is the same: draw all consistent arrangements and check each conclusion against **every** possibility.

Chain the statements: 'All A are B, All B are C' → A inside B inside C, so 'All A are C' follows. But 'Some C are A' may not follow if C could be larger. Test the tricky 'some/some not' conclusions carefully.
More statements = more circles, same rule: valid only if true in all arrangements. Chained 'All' statements are transitive; 'Some' statements rarely give definite 'All' conclusions.

mcqs.q: 'All A are B' and 'All B are C' together imply:
mcqs.explain: Transitivity: A inside B inside C means all A are C.

mcqs.q: Adding a third statement changes the method how?
options: Same Venn method with more circles/relationships
mcqs.explain: The approach is identical; there are just more relationships to diagram.

mcqs.q: 'All A are B, All B are C' does NOT necessarily imply:
mcqs.explain: 'All C are A' need not hold — C could contain elements outside A.

u:apt-130-possibility-cases.title: Possibility cases
u:apt-130-possibility-cases.summary: A 'possibility' conclusion is valid if at least one consistent diagram makes it true.

blocks.text: Some syllogism conclusions are phrased as **possibilities** ('Some A being C is a possibility'). Unlike definite conclusions, a possibility is valid if it can be true in **at least one** consistent diagram (not necessarily all).

Definite conclusion → must be true in ALL cases. Possibility conclusion → CAN be true in AT LEAST ONE case. So a possibility fails only if it's impossible in every valid diagram (e.g. contradicted by 'No A are C').

Flip the logic for possibilities: valid if achievable in some arrangement. It's invalid only when the statements make it impossible. Distinguish carefully between 'definitely follows' and 'is a possibility'.

mcqs.q: A 'possibility' conclusion in a syllogism is valid if it:
options: Must be true in all cases
Can be true in at least one consistent diagram
mcqs.explain: Possibility only requires achievability in some valid arrangement.

mcqs.q: A possibility conclusion is INVALID only when it is:
mcqs.explain: If no valid diagram allows it (e.g. contradicted by the premises), the possibility fails.

mcqs.q: Compared to a definite conclusion, a possibility conclusion needs:
options: Just one case where it holds
mcqs.explain: Definite needs all; possibility needs only one supporting arrangement.

u:apt-131-venn-method.title: Venn method
u:apt-131-venn-method.summary: The universal syllogism tool: draw circles for each set and test conclusions against all layouts.

blocks.text: The **Venn diagram method** is the safest, most systematic way to solve any syllogism. Represent each set as a circle, arrange them to satisfy the statements, and test conclusions against **all** valid arrangements.

items: 'All A are B' → A inside B. 'No A are B' → disjoint. 'Some A are B' → overlap. 'Some A are not B' → part of A outside B.
Try to draw a diagram where the conclusion is FALSE; if you can, it doesn't follow.
Use only the statements — no assumptions.

blocks.text: The winning strategy: try to make each conclusion FALSE with a legal diagram. If you can't (it's true in every case), it follows. This 'seek a counterexample' approach avoids the intuition traps syllogisms set.

mcqs.q: The most reliable technique for syllogisms is:
mcqs.explain: Diagrams systematically check whether a conclusion holds in every valid case.

mcqs.q: A good strategy is to try to draw a diagram where the conclusion is:
mcqs.explain: If a legal counterexample exists, the conclusion does not necessarily follow.

mcqs.q: 'Some A are not B' is drawn as:
mcqs.explain: At least some of A lies outside B.

u:apt-132-painted-cube-counting.title: Painted cube counting
u:apt-132-painted-cube-counting.summary: A painted n-cube cut into unit cubes: count faces painted by position (corner/edge/face/inner).

blocks.text: A cube with side **n** units, painted on all faces then cut into unit cubes, gives n^3 small cubes classified by how many faces are painted:
For n=4: 3-face = 8, 2-face = 12x2 = 24, 1-face = 6x4 = 24, 0-face = 2^3 = 8 (total 64 = 4^3). Corners always 8, regardless of n.
Memorise the four formulas. Corners = 8 (always), edges = 12(n-2), faces = 6(n-2)^2, interior = (n-2)^3. They sum to n^3.

mcqs.q: A painted cube cut into unit cubes always has how many cubes with exactly 3 painted faces?
mcqs.explain: The 8 corner cubes each have 3 painted faces, for any n.

mcqs.q: For a cube of side n, the number of cubes with exactly 1 painted face is:
mcqs.explain: Face-centre cubes number 6 faces x (n-2)^2 each.

mcqs.q: The number of completely unpainted (interior) cubes is:
mcqs.explain: The inner cube of side (n-2) has (n-2)^3 unpainted cubes.

u:apt-133-dice-opposite-faces.title: Dice opposite faces
u:apt-133-dice-opposite-faces.summary: Use two views to deduce opposite faces; on a standard die opposite faces sum to 7.

blocks.text: **Dice problems** give one or two views and ask which face is opposite another. On a **standard die, opposite faces sum to 7** (1-6, 2-5, 3-4). For non-standard dice, use two views: a face appearing in both views is NOT opposite the faces around it.

Two-view rule: if a common face appears in both positions, the two 'new' faces from each view (that aren't the common one and aren't already matched) are opposite each other. Rotate mentally or use the common-face method.
Standard die: opposite faces sum to 7. General dice: a face seen in two different views is adjacent (not opposite) to the other visible faces; deduce the opposite by elimination.

mcqs.q: On a standard die, the face opposite 2 is:
mcqs.explain: Opposite faces sum to 7, so 2 is opposite 5.

mcqs.q: On a standard die, opposite faces always sum to:
mcqs.explain: 1-6, 2-5, 3-4 each sum to 7.

mcqs.q: A face that appears in two different views of a die is ______ the other visible faces.
mcqs.explain: A common face is adjacent to the faces around it, helping deduce the opposite by elimination.

u:apt-134-cube-folding.title: Cube folding
u:apt-134-cube-folding.summary: From a flat net, determine which faces become opposite when folded into a cube.

blocks.text: **Cube folding** gives a flat **net** (unfolded cube) and asks which faces end up opposite or adjacent when folded. Key rule: in a net, faces that are **one square apart in a straight line** (with one between them) become **opposite** faces.

In a cross-shaped net, the centre square is adjacent to its four neighbours, and the top/bottom arms fold to be opposite each other. Faces directly next to each other in the net are adjacent (not opposite) in the cube.
Adjacent-in-net → adjacent-in-cube; one-square-gap-in-a-line → opposite. Mentally fold or use these adjacency rules to match faces. A face can't be opposite one it directly touches in the net.

mcqs.q: In a cube net, faces that are directly adjacent become ______ in the cube.
mcqs.explain: Touching faces in the net remain adjacent after folding.

mcqs.q: Faces one square apart in a straight line (with one between) fold to be:
mcqs.explain: A gap of one square along a line places the two faces opposite in the cube.

mcqs.q: A face can be opposite a face it directly touches in the net:
mcqs.explain: Directly adjacent net faces are always adjacent (never opposite) in the folded cube.

u:apt-135-single-row.title: Single row
u:apt-135-single-row.summary: Seat people in a line from clues; fix positions relative to a reference and account for facing.

blocks.text: **Single-row (linear) arrangement**: people sit in a line, all facing the same way. Place them using positional clues ('A is 2nd from left', 'B is immediately right of C'). Note whether they face North or South, which flips left/right.

If all face North, 'left' is toward the west end; if they face South, left/right reverse. Start from a definite clue (an end position or a fixed pair), then build outward. Draw the row with numbered positions.
Anchor on the most concrete clue, then place others relative to it. Track the facing direction carefully — it determines which side 'left' and 'right' mean.

mcqs.q: In a single-row arrangement, what determines which side is 'left'?
mcqs.explain: Facing North vs South flips the meaning of left and right.

mcqs.q: The best starting point is:
options: A definite clue (an end position or fixed pair)
mcqs.explain: Anchoring on a concrete clue lets you place others relative to it.

mcqs.q: If all face South, compared to facing North their left and right are:
mcqs.explain: Turning around swaps the left and right sides.

u:apt-136-two-rows-facing-each-other.title: Two rows facing each other
u:apt-136-two-rows-facing-each-other.summary: Two parallel rows face each other; person A in one faces the person opposite in the other.

blocks.text: In a **two-row (facing) arrangement**, two equal rows sit facing each other. Each person in one row faces a specific person in the other. Left/right differ between the rows because they face opposite directions.

If Row 1 faces North (South-side of the table) and Row 2 faces South, then Row 1's left is Row 2's right. 'A faces B' means they're directly opposite. Use 'faces' clues to link the two rows position by position.
Draw both rows aligned so opposite people line up. Remember the two rows face opposite ways, so their left/right are mirrored. 'Faces' links positions across the rows.

mcqs.q: In two rows facing each other, 'A faces B' means A and B are:
options: Directly opposite in the two rows
mcqs.explain: Facing links a person in one row to the one directly across.

mcqs.q: The left/right of the two rows are:
mcqs.explain: Since the rows face opposite ways, one row's left is the other's right.

mcqs.q: To solve these, you should draw:
options: Both rows aligned so opposite people line up
mcqs.explain: Aligning the two rows makes the facing relationships clear.

u:apt-137-with-attribute-matching.title: With attribute matching
u:apt-137-with-attribute-matching.summary: Arrangements plus extra attributes (job, colour) - build a grid to match each person to attributes.

blocks.text: Harder arrangements add **attributes** (each person also has a profession, favourite colour, city, etc.). Use a **grid/table** linking positions to people to attributes, filling cells as clues confirm or eliminate them.

Combine the seating diagram with an attribute table. A clue like 'the doctor sits to the left of the person who likes red' links seating and attributes — cross off impossible combinations systematically.
Track two layers: the arrangement AND the attributes. A grid (people vs attributes) plus the seating diagram, updated by elimination, cracks these multi-variable puzzles.

mcqs.q: For arrangement puzzles with extra attributes, the best tool is:
options: A grid/table linking positions, people, and attributes
mcqs.explain: A grid tracks the multiple variables and lets you eliminate combinations.

mcqs.q: Clues linking seating and attributes are handled by:
options: Cross-referencing the seating diagram with the attribute table
mcqs.explain: You connect the two layers, eliminating impossible pairings.

mcqs.q: Progress in these puzzles comes mainly through:
mcqs.explain: Ruling out options via the grid narrows down the unique solution.

u:apt-138-facing-centre.title: Facing centre
u:apt-138-facing-centre.summary: In a circle facing the centre, each person's left is the next clockwise neighbour.

blocks.text: In a **circular arrangement facing the centre**, for each person, their **left is clockwise** and their **right is anticlockwise** (from an observer's outside view it looks reversed). Place people around a circle using the neighbour clues.
When facing the centre, 'immediate left' means the next person clockwise. Fix one person, then place others by their left/right clues, going around the circle. Draw the circle and mark positions.
Facing centre: left = clockwise, right = anticlockwise (for the seated person). This is the opposite of what an outside observer sees, so anchor to the seated person's perspective.

mcqs.q: When people face the centre of a circle, a person's immediate left is the neighbour who is:
mcqs.explain: Facing inward, the person's left side corresponds to the clockwise direction.

mcqs.q: For circular puzzles, you should:
options: Draw a circle and mark positions from a fixed reference
mcqs.explain: A circle diagram anchored on one person handles the left/right relations.

mcqs.q: Facing the centre, the seated person's right is:
mcqs.explain: For someone facing inward, their right is the anticlockwise direction.

u:apt-139-facing-outward.title: Facing outward
u:apt-139-facing-outward.summary: Facing away from the centre reverses left/right: left is anticlockwise.

blocks.text: When people **face outward** (away from the centre), the left/right directions **reverse** compared to facing inward: a person's **left is anticlockwise** and **right is clockwise**.
Puzzles often mix inward- and outward-facing people; you must apply the correct left/right rule per person. For an outward-facer, 'immediate left' is the next person going anticlockwise.
Facing outward flips it: left = anticlockwise, right = clockwise. Always check each person's facing direction before interpreting their left/right clues.

mcqs.q: When facing outward from a circle, a person's left is toward the:
mcqs.explain: Facing outward reverses the inward case, so left is anticlockwise.

mcqs.q: Compared to facing the centre, facing outward:
mcqs.explain: Turning to face outward swaps the left and right sides.

mcqs.q: In mixed-facing circles, you must:
options: Apply the correct left/right rule per person's facing
mcqs.explain: Each person's facing determines how to read their left/right clues.

u:apt-140-mixed-facing.title: Mixed facing
u:apt-140-mixed-facing.summary: Some face in, some face out - apply each person's own left/right rule carefully.

blocks.text: **Mixed-facing** circular puzzles have some people facing the **centre** and others facing **outward**. For each clue, you must apply that specific person's left/right convention. This is the trickiest arrangement type.
Mark each person's facing (in/out) on your diagram. For an inward-facer, left = clockwise; for an outward-facer, left = anticlockwise. A clue about A's left depends on which way A faces.
Annotate facing direction for everyone first, then interpret each left/right clue from that person's own perspective. Consistency in applying per-person rules is what these puzzles test.

mcqs.q: In mixed-facing circles, a clue about someone's left depends on:
options: Whether that specific person faces inward or outward
mcqs.explain: Left/right is relative to each person's facing direction.

mcqs.q: The first step in mixed-facing puzzles is to:
options: Mark each person's facing direction on the diagram
mcqs.explain: Knowing each facing lets you correctly read their left/right clues.

mcqs.q: For an outward-facing person in the circle, immediate left is:
mcqs.explain: Outward-facers have left = anticlockwise (reversed from inward).

u:apt-141-with-attributes.title: With attributes
u:apt-141-with-attributes.summary: Circular seating plus attributes - combine the circle diagram with an attribute grid.

blocks.text: Advanced circular puzzles add **attributes** (profession, age, colour) to each seated person. Combine the **circle diagram** with an **attribute grid**, using elimination to match positions, people, and attributes.
Handle the seating (with facing) and the attributes together. A clue like 'the teacher sits opposite the person who likes blue' links both layers — narrow down by cross-referencing systematically.
Two-layer problem: circular positions AND attributes. Maintain the circle diagram plus an attribute table, and eliminate impossible pairings until the arrangement is unique.

mcqs.q: Circular puzzles with attributes are best solved using:
options: The circle diagram plus an attribute grid, with elimination
mcqs.explain: Two layers (seating and attributes) need both a diagram and a table.

mcqs.q: Clues linking position and attribute are resolved by:
mcqs.explain: Connecting seating and attributes through elimination pins down the solution.

mcqs.q: These puzzles are cracked mainly by:
mcqs.explain: Ruling out impossible combinations narrows to the unique arrangement.

u:apt-142-ranking.title: Ranking
u:apt-142-ranking.summary: 'Position from top and bottom' - total = positions from both ends minus 1.

blocks.text: **Ranking/position** problems: if a person is **a-th from the top** and **b-th from the bottom**, the **total number = a + b - 1** (the person is counted in both, so subtract 1).
If Ravi is 7th from the top and 12th from the bottom, total students = 7 + 12 - 1 = 18. To find a rank from the other end: rank from bottom = total - rank from top + 1.
Total = (rank from one end) + (rank from other end) - 1. The '-1' avoids double-counting the person. This single formula solves most ranking questions.

mcqs.q: A person is 5th from the top and 9th from the bottom. Total number of people is:
mcqs.explain: 5 + 9 - 1 = 13 (subtract 1 for double-counting the person).

mcqs.q: The ranking formula is total =
mcqs.explain: Subtract 1 because the person is counted from both ends.

mcqs.q: In a row of 20, a person 8th from the left is which from the right?
mcqs.explain: Rank from right = 20 - 8 + 1 = 13th.

u:apt-143-floor-puzzles.title: Floor puzzles
u:apt-143-floor-puzzles.summary: Assign people to numbered floors from above/below clues - build a vertical grid.

blocks.text: **Floor puzzles** assign people to numbered floors (e.g. 1 to 7) using clues like 'A lives above B', 'C is on an even floor', 'exactly 2 floors between D and E'. Build a **vertical list** of floors and place people by elimination.
Start with the most restrictive clue (a fixed floor, or 'top/bottom floor'). 'Exactly n floors between' means a gap of n+1 in floor numbers. Test cases where a clue allows two positions.
Treat floors as a numbered column; anchor on definite clues, then use 'above/below' and 'gap' clues to place everyone. Systematic elimination (and case-testing when needed) yields the arrangement.

mcqs.q: 'Exactly 3 floors between A and B' means their floor numbers differ by:
mcqs.explain: n floors between means a difference of n+1 = 4 in floor numbers.

mcqs.q: The best clue to start a floor puzzle with is:
options: The most restrictive (a fixed or top/bottom floor)
mcqs.explain: Anchoring on a definite position limits possibilities early.

mcqs.q: Floor puzzles are best represented as:
options: A vertical numbered list of floors
mcqs.explain: A vertical column matches the floors and makes above/below clues clear.

u:apt-144-scheduling-puzzles.title: Scheduling puzzles
u:apt-144-scheduling-puzzles.summary: Assign events to days/times from order and gap clues - use a timeline grid.

blocks.text: **Scheduling puzzles** assign items (people, events, meetings) to days, months, or time slots using ordering and gap clues ('X is before Y', 'exactly one day between A and B'). Use a **timeline/grid** and eliminate systematically.
List the slots (days/months) in order, anchor on fixed clues, and apply before/after and gap constraints. 'At least two days after' sets a minimum gap; test multiple cases when a clue is flexible.
Same technique as floor/arrangement puzzles: an ordered grid of slots, anchored on definite clues, filled by elimination and case-testing. Ordering and gap clues are the building blocks.

mcqs.q: Scheduling puzzles are best solved with:
options: An ordered timeline/grid filled by elimination
mcqs.explain: A grid of ordered slots with elimination handles the ordering and gap clues.

mcqs.q: 'At least two days after' sets a:
mcqs.explain: 'At least' fixes a lower bound on the gap, allowing more.

mcqs.q: When a clue permits more than one placement, you should:
mcqs.explain: Case-testing flexible clues, then checking consistency, resolves the arrangement.

u:apt-145-tournament-logic.title: Tournament logic
u:apt-145-tournament-logic.summary: Round-robin plays C(n,2) matches; a single-elimination knockout always needs exactly n-1 matches.

blocks.text: Two formats dominate these questions. In a **round-robin**, every player meets every other once, so the number of matches is **C(n,2) = n(n-1)/2**. In a **single-elimination knockout**, every match eliminates exactly one player, and you must eliminate all but the champion, so you always need **n-1 matches** for n players.

The knockout shortcut is format-independent: byes, seedings, and bracket shape do not change it. To crown 1 winner from n players you must eliminate n-1 players, and each match removes exactly one. So matches = n-1, always.
In round-robin points questions, total points distributed = (matches) x (points per match). With 2 points for a win, 1 each for a draw, the total is constant at 2 x C(n,2) no matter how games end.

mcqs.q: In a round-robin tournament with 8 teams, how many matches are played?
A knockout tournament has 64 players. How many matches decide the winner?
mcqs.explain: Each match eliminates one player; to leave one champion you eliminate 63, so 63 matches.

mcqs.q: In a round-robin, each of 5 teams plays every other once, 3 points per win and 1 each for a draw. What is the total number of matches?

u:apt-146-classic-interview-puzzles.title: Classic interview puzzles
u:apt-146-classic-interview-puzzles.summary: Learn the standard templates: bridge-and-torch, poison bottles, and light-bulb switches.

blocks.text: Interviewers reuse a small set of famous puzzles. Recognising the template is faster than solving from scratch.

items: **Bridge and torch:** to move a group across in minimum time, send the two fastest to shuttle the torch back, but for very different speeds it is often optimal to pair the two slowest together.
**Poison bottles / binary labelling:** to find 1 poisoned bottle among 1000 with test strips, give each bottle a binary ID and assign one strip per bit; 10 strips (2^10 = 1024) suffice.
**3 switches, 1 bulb:** turn switch 1 on for a while, turn it off, turn switch 2 on, enter the room. Lit = switch 2; off but warm = switch 1; off and cold = switch 3.

blocks.text: For 100 prisoners / hats and similar, the trick is usually a parity code or a pre-agreed strategy that converts private information into one shared signal.

mcqs.q: To identify 1 poisoned bottle among 1000 using test strips (each result available together), the minimum number of strips is:
mcqs.explain: Binary IDs: 2^10 = 1024 >= 1000, so 10 strips can encode every bottle.

mcqs.q: With 3 switches outside and 1 bulb in a closed room (one visit allowed), you distinguish switches using:
options: The bulb's heat as a second signal
Only whether the bulb is on
mcqs.explain: Heat gives a second state: on, off-but-warm, off-and-cold covers all three switches.

mcqs.q: In bridge-and-torch, the reason two people must sometimes return is:
options: The torch must come back for the others
mcqs.explain: Only one torch exists and it must be carried back so the remaining people can cross.

u:apt-147-weighing-and-measuring-puzzles.title: Weighing and measuring puzzles
u:apt-147-weighing-and-measuring-puzzles.summary: Balance-scale problems use ternary (3-way) information; jug problems use combinations of the two capacities.

blocks.text: A **balance scale** gives three outcomes per weighing (left heavier, right heavier, equal), so k weighings distinguish up to **3^k** cases. That is why 12 balls with one odd (heavier or lighter, unknown) is solvable in 3 weighings: 3^3 = 27 covers the 24 possibilities.

Coin/ball puzzles: if the odd one is known to be heavier (or lighter), n weighings identify it among up to 3^n coins. If heavier-or-lighter is unknown, you lose a little capacity but 3 weighings still handle 12.
**Water-jug** puzzles: with jugs of capacities a and b (litres), you can measure any multiple of gcd(a,b). With a 3 L and a 5 L jug you can measure 1, 2, 3, 4 L because gcd(3,5) = 1.

items: Fill the 5 L jug; pour into the 3 L jug, leaving 2 L in the 5 L.
Empty the 3 L; pour the 2 L into it.
Fill the 5 L again, top up the 3 L (needs 1 L), leaving 4 L in the 5 L jug.

mcqs.q: Among 9 identical-looking coins, one is heavier. Minimum balance weighings to find it for sure:
mcqs.explain: Each weighing has 3 outcomes; 3^2 = 9 covers all coins, so 2 weighings suffice.

mcqs.q: With a 3-litre and a 5-litre jug, which quantity CANNOT be measured exactly?
mcqs.explain: gcd(3,5) = 1, so every integer up to the larger jug is measurable; there is no impossible small amount.

mcqs.q: A balance scale gives how many distinct outcomes per weighing?
mcqs.explain: Left down, right down, or balanced - three outcomes, giving 3^k reach in k weighings.

u:apt-148-assumptions.title: Assumptions
u:apt-148-assumptions.summary: An assumption is an UNSTATED premise the argument needs to be true; test it with negation.

blocks.text: An **assumption** is something the author takes for granted - not written down, but required for the conclusion to hold. It bridges the gap between the stated evidence and the conclusion.
The Negation Test: negate the candidate assumption. If the argument falls apart, it WAS a necessary assumption. If the argument survives, it was not.
Do not confuse an assumption with a conclusion or with new information. An assumption must be something the argument already relies on, not an extra fact that would merely help.

mcqs.q: "We should advertise on TV; it will boost our sales." Which is an assumption?
mcqs.explain: The plan only works if the audience is reachable via TV - an unstated necessary premise.

mcqs.q: The best tool to check whether a statement is a necessary assumption is:
options: Negate it and see if the argument collapses
See if it is the longest option
mcqs.explain: Negation test: a necessary assumption, when negated, breaks the argument.

mcqs.q: An assumption differs from a conclusion because it is:
mcqs.explain: Assumptions are the hidden support; conclusions are the explicit claim being argued for.

u:apt-149-conclusions.title: Conclusions
u:apt-149-conclusions.summary: A valid conclusion MUST follow from the given statements alone - no outside knowledge, no probably.

blocks.text: In 'conclusion' questions you decide what **definitely follows** from the passage. Stick strictly to what is stated; do not add real-world knowledge or assume trends will continue.

items: Reject anything with 'always', 'never', 'only', 'all' unless the passage is that absolute.
Reject predictions of the future unless the passage explicitly forecasts them.
Accept the mild restatement that is fully supported by the text.

blocks.text: The safest conclusion is usually the least dramatic one. Extreme wording is the most common trap.

mcqs.q: "All the students who studied passed. Ravi passed." What follows?
options: Nothing certain about whether Ravi studied
mcqs.explain: Studying guarantees passing, but passing does not guarantee studying - Ravi could have passed either way.

mcqs.q: A conclusion in critical reasoning must:
options: Follow necessarily from the given statements
Be probably true in the real world
mcqs.explain: Only what necessarily follows from the text counts; outside likelihood is irrelevant.

mcqs.q: Which wording is most likely to make a conclusion WRONG?
options: An absolute term like 'never' not supported by the text
mcqs.explain: Overreaching absolutes are the classic trap; supported restatements are safe.

u:apt-150-strengthen-and-weaken.title: Strengthen and weaken
u:apt-150-strengthen-and-weaken.summary: Strengthen = make the conclusion more likely (often by confirming the assumption); weaken = attack the link between evidence and conclusion.

blocks.text: To **strengthen** an argument, add a fact that supports its assumption or rules out an alternative explanation. To **weaken** it, introduce an alternative cause or show the evidence does not support the conclusion.
The strongest weakener usually attacks the CAUSAL link, not the data. 'Sales rose after the ad' is weakened by 'a competitor closed that month' - an alternative cause.
A weakener does not need to disprove the conclusion outright; it only has to make it less likely. Likewise a strengthener need not prove it.

mcqs.q: "Crime fell after we added streetlights, so lights cut crime." Which WEAKENS this most?
options: Police patrols also doubled that year
mcqs.explain: An alternative cause (more patrols) undermines the claimed link between lights and the fall in crime.

mcqs.q: To strengthen an argument you typically:
options: Confirm its key assumption or rule out other causes
mcqs.explain: Supporting the hidden assumption or eliminating rival explanations bolsters the conclusion.

mcqs.q: A good weakener most often works by:
options: Offering an alternative explanation for the evidence
Proving the conclusion false with certainty
mcqs.explain: Alternative causes break the evidence-to-conclusion link, which is enough to weaken it.

u:apt-151-cause-and-effect.title: Cause and effect
u:apt-151-cause-and-effect.summary: Correlation is not causation; watch for reverse causation, common cause, and coincidence.

blocks.text: Cause-effect questions ask you to judge whether one event caused another. Two things happening together (correlation) does not prove one caused the other.

items: **Reverse causation:** maybe the effect actually caused the 'cause'.
**Common cause:** a third factor drives both (ice-cream sales and drownings both rise with heat).
**Coincidence:** with enough variables, some will correlate by chance.

blocks.text: For 'is A the cause and B the effect' item pairs, check the time order (cause precedes effect) and whether a plausible mechanism exists.

mcqs.q: Ice-cream sales and drowning deaths both rise in summer. The best explanation is:
mcqs.explain: Heat independently raises both - a classic common-cause (confounder) example.

mcqs.q: 'Correlation does not imply causation' warns against ignoring:
options: Reverse causation, common cause, and coincidence
mcqs.explain: These three alternatives explain a correlation without a direct cause-effect link.

mcqs.q: For A to be the cause of B, a minimum requirement is that:
mcqs.explain: A cause must precede its effect in time; without that, causation is impossible.

u:apt-152-two-set-problems.title: Two-set problems
u:apt-152-two-set-problems.summary: Inclusion-exclusion: n(A or B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A and B).

blocks.text: For two overlapping groups, the count in **either** set is n(A) + n(B) minus the overlap counted twice: **n(A U B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A n B)**.
'Only A' = n(A) - n(A n B). 'Neither' = Total - n(A U B). Sketch the two circles and fill the middle first.
